title: Chemistry in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what chemistry studies: what things are made of and how they change.
summary: Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes. People practiced it with fire long before it was a science, and today it connects to nearly every other science.

cards.headline: Your ancestors were chemists. They just didn't know it.
cards.body: Every time someone cooked over a fire, baked a clay pot or pulled metal out of rock, they were changing what stuff is made of. Nobody called it chemistry. So what exactly is it?

cards.fact: Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes.
cards.context: Textbooks say it more formally: the composition, properties and interactions of matter. Composition is what something is made of. Properties are how it looks and behaves, like how hard it is or whether it burns. Interactions are what happens when one kind of stuff meets another. The first cooks, potters and metalworkers were asking all three questions, with fire as their only lab equipment.

mascot.line: Middle of the room, and very happy to be there. Welcome to the tree!

cards.headline: The central science
cards.body: Chemistry is sometimes called the central science, because so many other fields lean on it: medicine, materials science, forensics, environmental science. Biology meets it in biochemistry, the study of the substances inside living things and how they change. Digesting your lunch, making the fibers in your clothes and the plastic in your credit card, refining crude oil into gasoline: all chemistry. Whatever science you love, chemistry is standing in the middle of the room.

title: What Matter Is
objective: After this level you can explain matter as anything that has mass and takes up space.
summary: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space, even air: a small room holds about 60 kg of it. Mass is how much matter there is; weight is the pull of gravity on it.

cards.headline: The air in a small bedroom has a mass of about 60 kilograms.
cards.body: You can't see it, and you walk straight through it. Yet it has mass, just like the bed. So what makes something count as matter?

cards.fact: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
cards.context: Those are the two tests. An ant passes them, and so do a truck, the Earth and a whole galaxy. Gases pass too, even invisible ones: if gas didn't take up space, blowing into a balloon wouldn't make it bigger. Remember Level 1? Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes. This is its raw material.

mascot.line: Don't worry. It has never once asked for rent.

cards.headline: Weighing a room full of air
cards.body: A liter of dry air has a mass of only about 1.2 grams. But rooms hold a lot of liters. A small bedroom, 4 meters by 5 meters with a 2.5-meter ceiling, holds 50,000 liters of air, about 60 kilograms of it. You've been sharing your room with a heavyweight all along.

cards.headline: Mass isn't weight
cards.body: Mass is how much matter something contains. Weight is the pull of gravity on that matter. Send an astronaut to the Moon, where gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, and she weighs one-sixth as much. Her mass doesn't change at all: same astronaut, same matter, lighter footsteps.
cards.callout: Mass: how much matter. Weight: how hard gravity pulls on it.

title: Solid, Liquid, Gas
objective: After this level you can explain the three everyday states of matter.
summary: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow but keep their volume, and gases fill their container. The difference comes from how tightly packed and how free the particles are.

cards.headline: Pour juice into a glass and it changes shape. It doesn't change amount.
cards.body: Try that with a brick and nothing happens. Let the air out of a balloon and it spreads through the whole room. Three kinds of matter, three very different behaviors. Why?

cards.headline: It's all in the particles
cards.body: All matter is made of tiny particles: atoms, often joined into molecules. In a solid, the particles are packed tight, often in a neat pattern, and just vibrate in place. In a liquid, they stay close together but slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and move on their own, meeting only when they collide. Same particles, different freedom.

mascot.line: I'm a dance-floor particle myself. Always moving, never leaving the party.

cards.headline: Picture a crowd (an analogy)
cards.body: A solid is like a stadium crowd in their seats: packed in, jiggling, going nowhere. A liquid is like a busy dance floor: everyone touching, everyone moving past each other, so the crowd takes the shape of the room. A gas is like a few kids let loose in a huge park, far apart, bumping into each other now and then. Seats keep their shape. Dancers don't.
cards.callout: Analogy: seats = solid, dance floor = liquid, open park = gas

title: Melting and Boiling
objective: After this level you can explain what happens to particles when things melt or boil.
summary: Heat speeds particles until they break free: solids melt, liquids boil. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level but about 90 °C high in the Rockies, because boiling depends on air pressure.

cards.headline: High in the Rocky Mountains, water boils at about 90 °C.
cards.body: It bubbles away just like a pot at the beach, yet it's about 10 degrees cooler. To see why, start with what heat does to particles.

cards.headline: Heat makes particles move
cards.body: Heating something gives its particles more energy, so they move faster. Heat a solid enough and its particles jiggle so hard they break out of their fixed places and start sliding past each other: it melts. Keep heating the liquid and particles break away from their neighbors entirely and fly off as a gas: it boils. Remember Level 3's stadium? Melting is the crowd leaving its seats.

mascot.line: Crank the burner all you like. At sea level, that pot still tops out at 100 °C.

cards.fact: Ice melts at 0 °C, and water boils at 100 °C at sea-level air pressure.
cards.context: Ice, liquid water and steam are the same substance, water, in different states. And here's an odd detail: while ice is melting or water is boiling, its temperature stays put. The heat goes into pulling particles apart, not into speeding them up. So an open pot boiling at sea level stays at 100 °C, however high you turn the burner.

cards.headline: Why mountains boil cooler
cards.body: Boiling isn't only about heat. A liquid boils when its vapor pushes out as hard as the air pressing down on it. High up there's less air overhead, so water needs less heat to push back. In Leadville, Colorado, about 3,100 meters up, that's about 90 °C. Melting points shift with pressure too, but only slightly. A boiling point always comes with a pressure attached.
cards.callout: Less air pressure, lower boiling point

title: Plasma
objective: After this level you can explain plasma, the state of matter in lightning and the Sun.
summary: Heat a gas enough, or hit it with lightning, and electrons break free, making plasma: a gas of charged particles. Stars are mostly plasma, so nearly all visible matter is plasma.

cards.headline: Lightning heats air to about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
cards.body: The air in a lightning channel can reach about 50,000 °F. That air stops being an ordinary gas and becomes a fourth state of matter, one you rarely meet on Earth but the universe is full of.

cards.fact: Plasma is a gas with its electrons torn loose.
cards.context: Heat a gas enough and its atoms crash together so hard that electrons, tiny charged particles from inside atoms, get knocked free. High-voltage electricity like lightning can do the same. What's left is a gas full of electrically charged particles, so plasma conducts electricity. Chemists count it as the fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid and gas.

mascot.line: Solid, liquid, gas: the local specials. Plasma is the house favorite.

cards.headline: Rare here, everywhere out there
cards.body: The Sun and the other stars are mostly plasma. That makes plasma the most common state of visible matter in the universe: nearly all of it. (That counts ordinary matter, not the mysterious dark matter.) Down here you catch plasma in flashes: lightning, and the glowing curtains of the aurora near the poles. The state you met last is the one the universe uses most.

cards.headline: One more rung on the energy ladder
cards.body: Remember Level 4: heat makes particles move faster, and melting and boiling are particles breaking free of each other. Plasma is the next rung up. Heat a gas far enough and the breaking goes deeper: electrons break away from their atoms. Solid, liquid, gas, plasma. Each step up is paid for in energy.
cards.callout: Solid → liquid → gas → plasma: more energy at every step

title: Mixtures and Solutions
objective: After this level you can explain how mixtures and solutions differ.
summary: A mixture mingles two or more kinds of matter in amounts that can vary. A cookie is patchy (heterogeneous); a solution is the same throughout, like salt water, air or brass.

cards.headline: Air is a solution. So is brass.
cards.body: No liquid required. To see how a gas and a metal can both be solutions, start with a chocolate chip cookie.

cards.headline: A cookie is a mixture
cards.body: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled together, in amounts that can vary: more chips, fewer chips, still a cookie. That's the difference from a pure substance, which always has the same makeup. In a cookie you can see the parts, chips here and dough there. Chemists call that heterogeneous: not the same all the way through. Granite and a bottle of Italian dressing are the same kind of mixture.

cards.headline: Solutions: mixed all the way down
cards.body: Stir salt into water and the salt seems to vanish, and every sip is equally salty. That's a homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through, and chemists call it a solution. The substance that gets dissolved (the salt) is the solute. The one doing the dissolving (the water) is the solvent. You can keep adding salt, but only up to a limit.
cards.callout: Solute: what dissolves. Solvent: what does the dissolving.

mascot.line: Somewhere a brass doorknob is quietly being a solution. Respect.

cards.headline: Solutions don't have to be wet
cards.body: Air is a solution: mostly nitrogen and oxygen, evenly mixed. Brass is a solution too, copper and zinc blended evenly into one solid metal. Maple syrup and gasoline qualify as well. So a solution isn't about being a liquid. It's about being mixed so evenly that every part matches every other part.

title: Separating Mixtures
objective: After this level you can explain filtering, evaporating and distilling.
summary: Mixtures can be pulled apart using physical differences. A filter holds back sand but not dissolved salt; evaporating the water leaves the salt; distilling catches the vapor to make fresh water.

cards.headline: A bucket of sandy seawater: can you get the sand, salt and fresh water back out?
cards.body: It's a mixture, so yes. Level 6 said mixtures can be separated by physical means, without making anything new. The trick is to use a difference between the parts: size, or how easily each turns into a vapor. Three steps.

cards.headline: Step 1: filter out the sand
cards.body: A filter lets liquid through but holds back solid bits. Pour the sandy seawater through one and the sand stays behind, just as a coffee filter holds back the grounds. But the salt goes straight through. It's dissolved, spread out among the water, so there are no grains left to catch. Filtering alone can't make seawater drinkable.

mascot.line: Great news, we have salt! Less great news, the water has left the building.

cards.headline: Step 2: evaporate for the salt
cards.body: When salty water is heated, the water evaporates and the salt stays behind. In many parts of the world, table salt is made just this way, from seawater. Evaporation is the tool for getting a dissolved solid back out of a solution. There's one catch: the fresh water you wanted just drifted off into the air.

cards.headline: Step 3: distill to keep the water
cards.body: Distillation catches that vapor. The salty water is heated until the water turns to vapor, and the vapor is cooled so it turns back into liquid in a separate container. The salt stays behind, and fresh water collects at the other end. It works because the parts of a mixture turn to vapor at different temperatures. Aristotle noticed more than 2,300 years ago that evaporated seawater makes pure water.
cards.callout: Filter: size. Evaporate: keep the solid. Distill: keep the liquid.

title: Density
objective: After this level you can explain why some things float and others sink.
summary: Density is mass divided by volume. Things float when less dense than the liquid around them, so a log floats and a nail sinks. Ice is about 90 percent as dense as water, so it floats.

cards.headline: Solid water floats on liquid water. That's stranger than it sounds.
cards.body: Most substances pack tighter as they freeze, but water spreads out. That's why your ice cubes bob at the top of your drink. The explanation comes down to one idea: density.

cards.fact: Density is how much mass is packed into each bit of space.
cards.context: Divide an object's mass by its volume and you get its density. A kilogram of feathers and a kilogram of lead have exactly the same mass; the lead just crams it into far less space. Liquid water comes in at about 1 gram per cubic centimeter. Keep that number handy: it's the one everything gets compared to.

mascot.line: Heavy isn't the question. Packed is.

cards.headline: Float or sink? Compare densities
cards.body: Whether something floats doesn't depend on how heavy it is. It depends on density. If an object's average density is less than the liquid's, it floats; if it's denser, it sinks. That's why a huge log floats while a tiny iron nail sinks. The log is far heavier, but wood is less dense than water, and iron is denser.

cards.headline: Why ice floats
cards.body: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open, roomy pattern that spreads them farther apart than in the liquid. Same mass, more space, so lower density: ice is only about 90 percent as dense as liquid water. Less dense means it floats. But only a little less dense, so it floats low, with most of an ice cube or an iceberg riding below the surface.
cards.callout: Ice: about 0.92 g per cm³. Liquid water: about 1.0.

title: Physical or Chemical Change?
objective: After this level you can tell a physical change from a chemical one.
summary: A physical change alters form or state but not what a substance is; a chemical change makes something new. Clues like bubbles can mislead, and some cases, like dissolving salt, sit in a gray area.

cards.headline: Melt a candle or burn it. Only one makes something new.
cards.body: Melted wax is still wax. Burning wax is a different story: it reacts to form new substances, carbon dioxide and water. That difference is the whole idea of this level.

cards.headline: Physical change: same stuff, new look
cards.body: In a physical change, matter changes its form or state, but not what it is. Melting ice, boiling water, tearing paper, grinding something into powder: all physical. Every change of state from Levels 3 and 4 belongs here. Steam is still water. Confetti is still paper.

cards.headline: Chemical change: something new appears
cards.body: In a chemical change, at least one new substance forms. Iron rusting, a match burning, meat cooking, a banana turning brown: each leaves you with different matter from what you started with. Chemical changes are often harder to undo than physical ones. A dry nail doesn't go un-rusty.

mascot.line: Bubbles are a clue, not a confession.

cards.headline: Clues, not proof
cards.body: Chemists look for clues of a chemical change: an unexpected color change, a new smell, heat or light given off, or bubbles of gas. But clues can mislead. Boiling water bubbles furiously, yet no new substance forms; it's just water turning to vapor. The real test is always the same question: is there new stuff?

cards.headline: The gray areas
cards.body: The line isn't perfectly sharp. Salt dissolving in water is usually filed as physical, but the salt comes apart into charged particles in the water, and some chemists argue that counts as chemical. Reversibility isn't a sure test either: a rechargeable battery runs a chemical change backward every time you charge it. Some science educators call it more of a spectrum than a wall.
cards.callout: A useful guide, with a few honest gray areas

title: Checkpoint: Matter
objective: After this level you can explain states of matter, mixtures and the two kinds of change.
summary: Dry ice and snow sublime straight to gas; frost deposits straight from vapor. Both are physical changes. One polar view holds the chapter: iceberg, salty sea, air and the plasma Sun.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: some matter skips a step.
cards.body: You've watched solids melt and liquids boil. Now meet the shortcut: solids that turn straight into gas, and gas that turns straight into solid. Then zoom out and find the whole chapter in one view.

cards.headline: Sublimation: solid straight to gas
cards.body: Dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, never makes a puddle. At normal air pressure it turns straight from solid to gas, a change called sublimation. Snow and ice do it too, slowly, even below freezing, and faster in wind and in the thin air up high. Level 4's lesson returns: pressure changes how matter changes state.

mascot.line: Frost is water skipping the line. Very efficient, very sparkly.

cards.headline: Deposition: gas straight to solid
cards.body: Run it backward and you get deposition: a gas turning straight into a solid. Frost is the everyday example, water vapor from the air forming ice without ever being liquid first. Like melting and boiling, both shortcuts are physical changes. Frost is still water, just in a new state.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one view
cards.body: Stand at the edge of a polar sea. The iceberg is matter: it has mass and takes up space. It floats because ice is less dense than water, and dissolved salt makes seawater denser still. The sea is a solution, which distilling could turn into fresh water. The air is a solution too, and a gas. And the Sun overhead is plasma. Four states of matter, one view.

title: The Idea of Atoms
objective: After this level you can explain how the idea of atoms began with the ancient Greeks.
summary: In the 5th century BCE, Leucippus and Democritus reasoned that cutting matter must stop at uncuttable atoms moving through the void. Aristotle disagreed; proof waited until the 1800s.

cards.headline: Cut a crumb in half. Then again. How long can you keep going?
cards.body: Forever, said some ancient thinkers. Two Greeks said no: sooner or later you hit a piece too small to cut. They had no microscope and no lab, only an argument. It gave us the word atom.

cards.fact: In the 5th century BCE, Leucippus and his student Democritus said all matter is made of tiny particles called atoms.
cards.context: The name comes from the Greek for "indivisible" or "uncuttable": an atom was meant to be the last piece, the one no knife could split. Remember Level 3, where all matter turned out to be made of tiny particles? This is where that idea began, about 2,400 years ago.

cards.headline: An argument, not an experiment
cards.body: Their reasoning went like this. Suppose you could cut anything in half forever, and then imagine finishing the job. What is left? If it is specks of dust, you haven't finished cutting. If it is nothing at all, how could a pile of nothings add up to a crumb? So the cutting must stop somewhere: at the atom. Notice what is missing. These philosophers never tested their idea with an experiment; they argued it.
cards.callout: No lab, just logic

mascot.line: So a crumb is just a very long word. Delicious spelling.

cards.headline: Atoms and the void
cards.body: Democritus pictured atoms moving through empty space, the void, and differing only in shape, size, arrangement and position. Ancient writers compared them to letters: A differs from N in shape, and AN differs from NA in arrangement. A few letters spell every word. Even sweetness, Democritus said, exists only "by convention"; in reality there are just atoms and void.

cards.headline: The idea that waited
cards.body: Not everyone agreed. Aristotle rejected atoms: he held that matter could be divided forever and was made of fire, earth, air and water. A scientific atomic theory, one that explained how matter actually behaves, arrived only in the early 1800s. The Greeks had the right hunch. It just took a very long time to prove.

cards.body: A whole atom has no overall charge, because it has exactly as many electrons as protons: every plus is matched by a minus, like a ledger that always balances. The proton count is also the atom's ID card. Any atom with 6 protons is carbon, whatever else is going on inside it. Change the protons and you have a different element altogether.
cards.callout: Protons = identity. Electrons = balance.

mascot.line: Featherweights, yes. But keep an eye on them. They'll matter a lot in Level 14.

cards.fact: It takes about 1,800 electrons to match the mass of one proton.
cards.context: Protons and neutrons have almost the same mass, and each is far heavier than an electron. So nearly all of an atom's mass sits in its nucleus, the dense little center. Weigh an atom and you are really weighing its protons and neutrons; the electrons barely register. They are the featherweights of the atom.

title: How Small Is an Atom?
objective: After this level you can picture just how small an atom is.
summary: An atom is about a ten-billionth of a meter across: 50 million in a row make a centimeter. Its nucleus is 100,000 times smaller still, a blueberry in a stadium, so the atom is mostly empty space.

cards.headline: Draw a line 1 centimeter long. About 50 million atoms fit along it.
cards.body: Shoulder to shoulder, in a single row. Numbers like that stop meaning much, so this level trades them for pictures you can hold in your head.

cards.fact: An atom is about one ten-billionth of a meter across: 0.1 nanometers.
cards.context: The smallest marks on a ruler are millimeters, and a millimeter is ten million times wider than an atom that size. Look at the gap between two millimeter marks: ten million atoms would fit across it, side by side.

cards.headline: A blueberry in a stadium (true to scale)
cards.body: Now zoom inside. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the whole atom. Blow an atom up to the size of a football stadium and its nucleus would be a blueberry at the center of the field. The electrons have the rest: the stands, the roof, the parking lot.

mascot.line: One blueberry, carrying the whole stadium. Tiny, but it pulls its weight.

cards.headline: Mostly empty
cards.body: So by volume, an atom is mostly empty space, with its electrons occupying almost all of it. Yet Level 12 showed that the nucleus holds nearly all the mass. Put those together and you get the atom's great mismatch: the blueberry carries almost the entire mass of the stadium.

title: Electron Shells
objective: After this level you can explain how electrons fill shells around the nucleus.
summary: Electrons sit only in certain energy levels, or shells (Bohr, 1913). The first holds 2 and the second 8, filled from the inside out: sodium is 2, 8, 1. The outer shell decides how an atom behaves.

cards.headline: Sodium has 11 electrons. One of them sits alone.
cards.body: Ten are tucked in close to the nucleus. The eleventh is out on its own, farther away. Why the lopsided seating plan? Electrons don't just swarm around the nucleus anyhow. They fill shells.

cards.headline: Rungs, not a ramp
cards.body: In 1913, Niels Bohr explained that electrons can't sit at just any distance from the nucleus. They are allowed only certain energy levels, now called shells. Think of a ladder rather than a ramp: you can stand on a rung, never between two. Electrons take the lowest-energy spots first, in the shell closest to the nucleus, then work outward.
cards.callout: Analogy: shells are rungs on a ladder, not points on a ramp

mascot.line: Two, then eight. Say it like a phone number and it sticks.

cards.fact: The first shell holds up to 2 electrons; the second holds up to 8.
cards.context: Once a shell is full, the next electron has to start a new shell farther out. Neon has 10 electrons, exactly enough to fill the first two. Sodium has one more, 11, so its arrangement is 2, 8, 1: two full shells and a lone electron starting the third. Now the hook makes sense.

cards.headline: The outside does the talking
cards.body: The outermost shell, called the valence shell, decides how an atom behaves chemically. Neon, with its outer shell full, is stable and rarely bonds with anything. Sodium's lonely outer electron gives it a very different personality, a story for later chapters. When atoms meet, it's their outer shells that shake hands.

title: Isotopes
objective: After this level you can explain isotopes as atoms of one element with different masses.
summary: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons: carbon-12, -13 and -14 all have 6 protons. Same electrons means nearly the same chemistry.

cards.headline: Every carbon atom has 6 protons. They don't all weigh the same.
cards.body: Same element, same chemistry, different mass. The difference is hiding in the nucleus, among the particles with no charge.

cards.fact: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
cards.context: Add up an atom's protons and neutrons and you get its mass number, which goes in the isotope's name. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; carbon-13 has 7 neutrons, and carbon-14 has 8. All three are carbon, because all three have 6 protons. About 99 percent of natural carbon is carbon-12. Carbon-14 exists only in traces.

mascot.line: Same name on the door, different furniture inside.

cards.headline: Hydrogen's three versions
cards.body: Hydrogen, the simplest atom, has three isotopes, each with 1 proton. Ordinary hydrogen has no neutron at all. Deuterium has one, and tritium has two. Different masses, but all three are hydrogen: the proton count never changed.

cards.headline: Same place, same chemistry
cards.body: Isotopes of an element behave almost identically in chemical reactions. Level 14 explains why: chemistry is decided by the outer electrons, and a neutral atom's electron count matches its protons, not its neutrons. The name fits. In 1913 the doctor and writer Margaret Todd suggested "isotope", Greek for "same place", to the chemist Frederick Soddy: isotopes share one place in the periodic table.

title: Radioactivity
objective: After this level you can explain radioactive decay.
summary: Becquerel found radioactivity in 1896 when uranium fogged wrapped plates without sunlight. Unstable nuclei decay, giving off alpha, beta or gamma radiation, measured by half-life.

cards.headline: In 1896, some uranium salts took a picture in the dark.
cards.body: Henri Becquerel had wrapped photographic plates in paper that no light could get through, then set uranium salts on top. Something fogged the plates anyway. It wasn't light.

mascot.line: A cloudy day, a curious scientist, and a whole new field. Never skip developing the plates!

cards.headline: The cloudy-day discovery
cards.body: Becquerel thought sunlight made the uranium salts give off rays that could pass through paper. Then overcast Paris skies spoiled his experiment in February 1896. He developed the plates anyway, and the images were strong and clear. The uranium was giving off radiation all by itself, no sunlight needed. He had discovered radioactivity.

cards.fact: Radioactive decay: an unstable nucleus breaks down on its own, giving off radiation.
cards.context: Some isotopes are stable: left alone, they never change. Others have unbalanced nuclei, and each one eventually decays toward something more stable. That can turn it into a different atom altogether. Remember Level 12's ID card? Change the protons and you change the element.

cards.body: Every radioactive isotope has a half-life: the time it takes for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life, half remain. After two, a quarter. After three, an eighth. Depending on the isotope, a half-life can be mere seconds or billions of years.

title: Carbon Dating
objective: After this level you can explain how carbon dating tells the age of old things.
summary: Living things take in carbon-14 made by cosmic rays. After death it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years, dating remains up to about 50,000 years old: never dinosaurs.

cards.headline: Every living thing carries a clock. It starts when life stops.
cards.body: The clock is carbon-14, the rare radioactive isotope from Level 15. Here is how it tells the age of ancient wood and bone, and why it can't tell you a thing about a dinosaur.

cards.headline: Made in the sky
cards.body: Carbon-14 forms high in the atmosphere, where neutrons made by cosmic rays strike nitrogen atoms. It ends up in the air's carbon dioxide, which green plants absorb. Animals eat the plants, and other animals eat those animals. So every living thing keeps taking in carbon-14 for as long as it lives, including you.

mascot.line: Less carbon-14 left means a longer time since the clock started.

cards.fact: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.
cards.context: When an organism dies, it stops taking in carbon-14, and the amount in its remains steadily drops as it decays back into nitrogen. Measure what is left and you can work out how long ago it died: half the carbon-14 is gone after about 5,730 years, three-quarters after about 11,460. Willard Libby developed the method in the late 1940s and won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

cards.headline: Sorry, T. rex
cards.body: The clock has limits. It works only on things that were once alive, and only back to about 50,000 years; older remains have too little carbon-14 left to measure. The last non-bird dinosaurs died about 66 million years ago, more than 1,000 times beyond that reach. For them, geologists need clocks with much longer half-lives.

title: Seeing Atoms
objective: After this level you can explain how scientists can image single atoms.
summary: Light microscopes can't resolve anything much below 200 nanometers, far bigger than an atom. The scanning tunneling microscope (1981) maps single atoms by feeling a surface with a one-atom tip.

cards.headline: In 1989, two scientists wrote a company's name in 35 atoms.
cards.body: Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer spelled IBM with single xenon atoms on a nickel surface. To place atoms one by one, you first have to see them. No light microscope ever could.

cards.headline: Why light can't do it
cards.body: A light microscope can't separate details closer together than about half the wavelength of light: about 200 nanometers at best. An atom is about 0.1 nanometers across (Level 13), some 2,000 times smaller. Better lenses won't help. The limit comes from the physics of light itself.
cards.callout: Light microscope limit: about 200 nm. Atom: about 0.1 nm.

cards.fact: The scanning tunneling microscope, invented at IBM in 1981, can map single atoms.
cards.context: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built it at IBM's Zurich lab and won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. It uses no light at all. Instead, a needle whose tip narrows to a single atom scans across the surface, about two atoms' width above it, never touching.

mascot.line: Not a photograph, a fingertip map. Honestly, that's even cooler.

cards.headline: Feeling, not looking
cards.body: Close your eyes and run a finger along the tops of a row of books: you feel every change in height. The STM does the same with its tip (an analogy). A small voltage lets electrons jump the gap, and the tip moves up or down to keep that current steady. Its path becomes a map of the surface. Strictly, the map shows where the atoms' electrons are, not a photo of the atoms.

title: Finding the Atom's Parts
objective: After this level you can explain Thomson's and Rutherford's experiments.
summary: Thomson found the electron in 1897 and pictured a plum pudding atom. In 1909 alpha particles bounced back off gold foil, and in 1911 Rutherford explained it with a tiny, dense nucleus.

cards.headline: The day a shell bounced off tissue paper (almost)
cards.body: That is roughly how Ernest Rutherford described one result from his lab. To see why it stunned him, start with the atom everyone believed in before.

cards.headline: Thomson finds the electron
cards.body: In 1897, J.J. Thomson was studying cathode rays, made by driving electricity through a tube with most of the air pumped out. He concluded they were particles far lighter than any atom, and that all matter contains them. He called them corpuscles; we call them electrons. The uncuttable atom had a piece you could knock off.

cards.headline: The plum pudding
cards.body: Atoms carry no overall charge, so something positive had to balance those negative electrons. Thomson pictured a sphere of evenly spread positive matter with electrons stuck in it, like plums in a pudding. Positive charge everywhere, spread thin.
cards.callout: Plum pudding: spread-out positive, with electrons as the plums

cards.headline: The gold foil surprise
cards.body: In 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working with Rutherford, fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through. A very few bounced almost straight back, which the plum pudding couldn't explain. Rutherford said it was "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you."

mascot.line: Most shots sailed through, a few bounced back, and physics found the atom's heart.

cards.headline: A tiny, heavy heart
cards.body: In 1911 Rutherford explained it: an atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus, with electrons around it and mostly empty space between. Most alpha particles miss the nucleus entirely; the rare near-hits bounce back. In 1932, James Chadwick found the last piece: the neutron.

cards.headline: From orbits to clouds

Today an electron's home is an orbital: a region where it is most likely to be found. Shells survive as the layers where those clouds sit. title: Elements
objective: After this level you can explain what an element is.
summary: An element is a substance chemistry can't split into anything simpler; its atomic number (proton count) decides which one it is. Compounds like water join elements. There are 118.

cards.headline: Everything you've ever touched is built from 118 ingredients.
cards.body: Your phone, your breakfast and the air in your lungs are all made of elements, and chemists know just 118 of them. So what earns a substance a place on that list?

cards.fact: An element can't be broken down into anything simpler by chemistry.
cards.context: Water fails that test. Pass electricity through it and it comes apart into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. So water is a compound: a pure substance made of elements joined together. Hydrogen and oxygen can't be split any further, so they are elements. And notice the twist: water behaves nothing like either of the gases it's made from.

mascot.line: One number, one identity. Elements are wonderfully easy to ID.

cards.headline: What makes gold gold
cards.body: Deep in every atom sits a nucleus holding particles called protons. The number of protons is the atom's atomic number, and it decides which element the atom is. Every atom with 1 proton is hydrogen. Every atom with 8 is oxygen. Every atom with 79 is gold. Change the count and you've changed the element. An element's whole ID card is one number.

cards.headline: The purest stuff there is
cards.body: Remember Level 6: a pure substance always has the same composition, while a mixture can vary and be separated by physical means. Elements are pure substances, and so are compounds like water. Think of elements as an alphabet (an analogy): every compound is a word spelled with them. Water is a word spelled with just two letters, hydrogen and oxygen.

title: Mendeleev's Table
objective: After this level you can explain how Mendeleev arranged the elements and predicted new ones.
summary: In 1869 Mendeleev ordered elements by atomic weight, grouped look-alikes and left gaps for unknown elements, later filled by gallium, scandium and germanium. Today atomic number sets the order.

cards.headline: In 1869, a chemist left holes in his table on purpose.
cards.body: Dmitri Mendeleev was sorting the elements known in his day into a table. His boldest move wasn't what he put in. It was what he left out.

cards.headline: Sort by weight, group by behavior
cards.body: Mendeleev lined the elements up by increasing atomic weight and noticed that similar properties kept coming back in a pattern. So he placed the look-alikes together. In Germany, Lothar Meyer spotted the same pattern on his own and published a similar table in 1870. Two chemists, working separately, finding one pattern: a good sign the pattern was real.

mascot.line: Predicting an element before anyone finds it: the table showing off, in the best way.

cards.fact: Mendeleev left gaps for elements nobody had found, and predicted what they'd be like.
cards.context: Gallium turned up in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, each fitting a gap. Germanium was the showstopper. For the missing element he called eka-silicon, Mendeleev forecast an atomic weight of 72, a gray color and a high melting point. When Clemens Winkler found germanium in 1886, its atomic weight was 72.6. That is a description of a stranger, written years before you meet them.

cards.headline: One upgrade since 1869
cards.body: Mendeleev ordered by atomic weight, the best measure he had. In the 1910s, scientists realized the true order is atomic number, the proton count you met in Level 21. Today's periodic table runs in that order, all 118 elements of it, and the proton count is what gives each element its place.

title: Reading the Periodic Table
objective: After this level you can explain groups and periods on the periodic table.
summary: The table has 7 rows (periods) and 18 columns (groups). Properties repeat along the rows, the periodic law, so elements in a group behave alike. Each box shows atomic number, symbol and name.

cards.headline: The periodic table isn't a list. It's a map.
cards.body: Rows, columns, a number and a code in every box. It looks like a spreadsheet, but an element's address tells you a lot about how it behaves. Here's how to read it.

cards.headline: Rows and columns
cards.body: The table has 7 rows, called periods, and 18 columns, called groups, with the elements in order of atomic number. The columns are where the power is: elements in the same group tend to behave in similar ways. Neighbors in a column are family. Neighbors in a row are just, well, neighbors.

mascot.line: Periodic just means it repeats. Like Mondays, but more useful.

cards.headline: Why "periodic"?
cards.body: Lay the elements out in order and their properties keep coming back, the way Monday comes around every week. Chemists call this repeating pattern the periodic law, and it's where the table gets its name. Each row starts the cycle again, so elements that behave alike end up stacked in the same column.

cards.fact: Each box gives an element's atomic number, symbol and name, usually with its atomic mass.
cards.context: Symbols are one or two letters, and only the first is a capital: Co is cobalt, while CO is carbon monoxide. Some symbols only make sense in Latin. Iron is Fe, from ferrum. Gold is Au, from aurum. Lead is Pb, from plumbum. Old names, still printed on every chart.

title: Metals and Nonmetals
objective: After this level you can compare metals and nonmetals.
summary: About three-quarters of elements are metals: shiny, malleable conductors. Nonmetals at the upper right are dull, brittle, poor conductors. Metalloids sit between. Only mercury and bromine are liquid.

cards.headline: About three out of four elements are metals.
cards.body: Shiny, bendy, great at carrying heat and electricity: most of the periodic table is metal. The nonmetals gather in the upper right corner, and in many ways they behave like the opposite.

cards.headline: What makes a metal a metal
cards.body: Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable (you can hammer them into thin sheets) and ductile (you can draw them into wire). They're good conductors of heat and electricity, which is why a metal spoon left in hot soup soon gets hot. At room temperature they're solids, with one runny exception: mercury.

cards.headline: Nonmetals: the other corner
cards.body: Nonmetals tend to be dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors of heat and electricity. Most are gases or solids. On the map, metals fill the left side and the middle, nonmetals sit in the upper right, and along the staircase line between them live the metalloids, elements with in-between properties. Borderlands exist even on the periodic table.

mascot.line: Two puddles on the whole map. The periodic table is a mostly dry place.

cards.headline: Only two puddles
cards.body: Remember Level 3's solids, liquids and gases? Check every element at room temperature and you'll find plenty of solids and gases, but only two liquids: mercury, a metal, and bromine, a deep-red nonmetal. One puddle on each side of the staircase.

title: Noble Gases
objective: After this level you can explain why noble gases barely react, and how neon lights glow.
summary: Group 18's noble gases have complete outer shells, so they barely react. Neon signs glow because electricity turns the gas into plasma. Neon and argon are distilled from liquid air.

cards.headline: In 1894, two scientists found a new element hiding in air.
cards.body: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay pulled a gas out of the air that had been there all along, just under 1 percent of the atmosphere. They named it argon, from the Greek for idle, or lazy. It had earned the name.

cards.fact: Noble gases barely react with anything.
cards.context: Group 18 is helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon and oganesson: colorless, odorless gases that very rarely form compounds. The reason is inside the atom. Their outermost electron shells are already complete, so they have little reason to react. Chemists long called them inert, meaning totally unreactive, until 1962, when Neil Bartlett made a compound of xenon. Barely, it turns out, isn't never.

mascot.line: So the famous neon sign is really a plasma sign. Let's keep that between us.

cards.headline: Neon's glow is plasma
cards.body: Send electricity through neon gas in a sealed tube and it glows reddish orange. The current turns the gas into glowing plasma, Level 5's fourth state of matter: electrons torn loose from their atoms. Only the red signs hold real neon. Other colors come from other gases, such as argon and mercury. Every neon sign glows with plasma; not every one holds neon.

cards.headline: Harvested from air
cards.body: Where does neon come from? The same place Rayleigh and Ramsay found argon: the air. Neon and argon are separated from liquid air by distillation, Level 7's trick. Each part of a mixture boils at its own temperature, so the lazy gases come off one by one, ready to fill a tube.

title: Alkali Metals
objective: After this level you can explain why sodium and potassium react so violently with water.
summary: Group 1 alkali metals are soft and never found pure. With water they make hydrogen, a hydroxide and heat, more violently down the group, as the single outer electron gets easier to lose.

cards.headline: Some metals are soft enough to cut with a knife.
cards.body: Sodium is a real metal, silvery and shiny, yet you can cut it with a knife at room temperature. In water it fizzes, melts into a ball and skims across the surface. Meet group 1, the table's wildest column.

cards.fact: Alkali metals are so reactive that nature never keeps them pure.
cards.context: Group 1's alkali metals are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium and francium, all soft, silvery metals. Hydrogen sits on top of the column but isn't one of them. In nature, alkali metals are only ever found in compounds. The sodium in the sea, for example, is mostly locked up in dissolved sodium chloride.

cards.headline: Water brings out the wild side
cards.body: Every alkali metal reacts with water, making hydrogen gas and a hydroxide, a strong base also called an alkali. That's where the family gets its name. The reaction also gives off heat, and that heat matters for what comes next.

mascot.line: These are for chemists behind safety shields, not for kitchens. Admire them from the page.

cards.headline: Wilder down the column
cards.body: Go down the group and the reaction gets fiercer. Lithium fizzes steadily. Sodium melts into a ball that skims the surface. Potassium gives off enough heat to set the hydrogen alight. Rubidium reacts violently, and cesium explodes. Why? Each atom has a single outer electron it gives up easily, and lower in the column that electron sits farther from the nucleus, so it's even easier to lose.

cards.headline: One step past calm
cards.body: Neon's atomic number is 10; sodium's is 11. One more proton, and you go from the calmest gas on the table to a metal that fizzes in water. Neon's outer shell is complete. Sodium carries one lone outer electron, easy to give away. Next-door numbers, opposite personalities.

title: Halogens
objective: After this level you can describe chlorine and its relatives and how we use them.
summary: Group 17 halogens are reactive "salt formers"; fluorine is the most reactive element. They span gas, liquid and solid. Chlorine disinfects water; fluoride and iodide protect health.

cards.headline: A toxic gas helps keep your tap water safe.
cards.body: Chlorine is a toxic, yellow-green gas; its name comes from the Greek for greenish yellow. It also kills bacteria, which is why it goes into drinking water. Meet group 17, the halogens.

cards.fact: Halogen means "salt former" in Greek.
cards.context: Group 17 is fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine and tennessine. They're fiercely reactive nonmetals, each with seven outer electrons, one short of a full shell, and they readily grab one more. Pair a halogen with sodium and you get a salt; the best known, sodium chloride, is table salt. Fluorine is the most reactive element of all, and reactivity falls as you go down the group.

mascot.line: Gas, liquid, solid, all in one column. Level 3 would be proud.

cards.headline: Three states in one column
cards.body: At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a deep-red liquid and iodine is a shiny black solid. When iodine is warmed, it skips the liquid step and sublimes straight into a purple vapor, Level 10's shortcut. That violet cloud gave it its name: iodine comes from the Greek for violet.

cards.headline: Fierce elements on guard duty
cards.body: Chlorine kills bacteria, so it's used to treat drinking water and swimming pools. In 1908, Jersey City, New Jersey, became the first US city to routinely disinfect its drinking water, and along with better sanitation, disinfection helped typhoid and cholera cases drop dramatically. Fluorine compounds help prevent tooth decay, and a little iodide in table salt prevents iodine deficiency. Tamed, the fiercest family makes a fine bodyguard.

title: Making New Elements
objective: After this level you can explain how the heaviest elements are made in laboratories.
summary: Elements beyond uranium are made by people, starting with neptunium in 1940. Element 118 came from fusing calcium (20 protons) with californium (98). The 2016 names completed row seven.

cards.headline: Past uranium, element 92, nature almost runs out.
cards.body: Every element beyond uranium was first made by people, in reactors and particle accelerators. Only two of them turn up in nature, in tiny traces. So how do you build an element nobody has ever seen?

cards.headline: Neptunium: one step past uranium
cards.body: In 1940, Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson at Berkeley bombarded uranium with neutrons and made element 93. They named it neptunium, after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus, just as their element sat beyond uranium. Elements past uranium are called transuranium elements. All 26 known today are radioactive.

mascot.line: Months of work for three atoms. Chemistry has never been so patient.

cards.fact: Element 118 was made by fusing calcium (20 protons) with californium (98).
cards.context: In 2005, in Dubna, Russia, a Russian and American team fired calcium ions at a californium target at about 10 percent of the speed of light. Remember Level 21: the proton count decides the element. Nuclei almost never fuse, but when they did, 20 plus 98 made 118. From February to June, the experiment produced three atoms.

cards.headline: The seventh row, complete
cards.body: In 2016, IUPAC named the four newest elements: nihonium (113), moscovium (115), tennessine (117) and oganesson (118), completing the table's seventh row. Oganesson honors Yuri Oganessian, a pioneer of superheavy element research, who was alive to see it. Only a few atoms of oganesson have ever been made. Don't expect an oganesson ring.

title: Elements From Stars
objective: After this level you can explain how stars and supernovas made the elements.
summary: The Big Bang made hydrogen, helium and a little lithium. Stars fused heavier elements up to iron and scattered them. Heavier ones come from supernovas and neutron star collisions.

cards.headline: You are made of recycled stars.
cards.body: The carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and iron in your body were made inside stars. Labs build a few atoms at a time; the universe built the rest. To see how, start at the very beginning.

cards.headline: The Big Bang's short list
cards.body: The Big Bang made all of the universe's hydrogen, most of its helium and some lithium. Those are elements 1, 2 and 3, the first three boxes on the table. The hydrogen atoms in your glass of water were made in the Big Bang itself. Nearly every other element had to be built later, somewhere much hotter than a kitchen.

mascot.line: Every carbon atom in you had a star for a birthplace. Not a bad family tree.

cards.headline: Stars: element factories
cards.body: Stars shine by fusing light elements into heavier ones. Helium goes on to become carbon and oxygen, and so on, up to iron. When a giant star dies, it explodes and blows those elements out into space, where they become part of new stars, new planets and, eventually, you.

cards.headline: Beyond iron: explosions and collisions
cards.body: Fusion in stars can't make elements heavier than iron. Those need something more violent: a supernova explosion, or two neutron stars (the ultra-dense remains of dead stars) smashing together. In 2017, telescopes watched a neutron star merger that could have created gold and platinum. Level 28's lab fused nuclei to get three atoms; these collisions work on a cosmic scale.

title: Checkpoint: The Periodic Table
objective: After this level you can use the periodic table to predict how an element behaves.
summary: Metallic character grows toward the lower left and nonmetallic character toward the upper right, so an element's position predicts its behavior, as with rubidium. One map holds the whole chapter.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: predict an element you've never met.
cards.body: Mendeleev predicted germanium from a gap. Now you have the full map. By the end of this level, an element's address will tell you much of what it does.

cards.headline: Two fierce corners, one calm column
cards.body: Metallic character is strongest at the left of the table and grows as you go down a group, so the most metallic elements sit at the lower left. Nonmetallic character peaks at the upper right. That puts the fiercest reactors in opposite corners: cesium, which explodes in water, at the lower left, and fluorine, the most reactive element, at the upper right. Beside fluorine runs the calmest column of all, the noble gases.

cards.headline: Reading an address
cards.body: Try rubidium, in group 1 between potassium and cesium. Its column says soft, reactive metal; its place in the column says fiercer than potassium. That's exactly right: rubidium reacts violently with water. Or take tennessine, element 117, made only in labs. Its column files it with the halogens. That's Mendeleev's trick, played on a finished map.

mascot.line: One map, 118 elements, and now you can read it. Chapter 3, done.

cards.headline: The whole chapter on one map
cards.body: Elements are the substances chemistry can't split. Mendeleev lined them up and predicted the gaps; today atomic number sets the order. Metals fill the left, nonmetals the upper right. Group 1 fizzes, group 17 grabs, group 18 shrugs. The first three elements came from the Big Bang, others up to iron from stars, and heavier ones from exploding and colliding stars.

title: Hydrogen
objective: After this level you can describe hydrogen, the lightest and most common element.
summary: Hydrogen is the simplest element and over 90 percent of the universe's atoms. As the lightest gas it escapes Earth's air, so here it hides in water, which its name says it makes.

cards.headline: Nine out of every ten atoms in the universe are hydrogen.
cards.body: It's the most common element there is. Yet if you went looking for pure hydrogen gas in the air around you, you'd come up nearly empty-handed. Where did it all go?

cards.fact: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe: more than 90 percent of all atoms.
cards.context: It's also the simplest element of all, and by mass it makes up about three-quarters of the universe's ordinary matter. The runner-up, helium, isn't close: hydrogen is about three times as abundant. Picture the universe as a giant bag of marbles (an analogy, but a fair one): pull out ten, and nine or more are hydrogen.

mascot.line: The universe's most popular element, and Earth keeps letting it slip away.

cards.headline: The lightest gas there is
cards.body: Hydrogen is the lightest of all gases, about 14 times less dense than air. Remember Level 8's rule: less dense floats. Hydrogen plays the same trick in air, rising fast. High in the atmosphere its molecules move quickly enough to escape into space altogether. So free hydrogen is scarce in the air you breathe. Earth simply can't hold on to it.

cards.headline: The water maker
cards.body: So where is Earth's hydrogen? Mostly locked up in water: in oceans, ice, rivers and lakes. In 1766 Henry Cavendish showed that a gas that burns was a substance all its own. When it burns with oxygen, it forms water, so Lavoisier named it hydrogen, from Greek words meaning maker of water. The most common element in the universe spends its time on Earth hiding in your glass.

title: Oxygen
objective: After this level you can explain why oxygen matters for breathing and burning.
summary: Oxygen is 21 percent of the air and nearly half the crust. It reacts with almost everything, feeding both flames and cells. Its name, acid former, came from a mistake.

cards.headline: In 1774, one new gas made a candle flare and a mouse thrive.
cards.body: Joseph Priestley had made a new kind of air. A candle burned more vigorously in it, and a mouse did well in it too. One gas was feeding both a flame and a living thing. What was it, and why does so much depend on it?

cards.fact: Oxygen makes up 21 percent of the air, by volume.
cards.context: That's about a fifth of every breath you take in. But the air isn't where most of Earth's oxygen lives. Bound up in rocks, oxygen is the most plentiful element in Earth's crust, nearly half of it by weight. The ground under your feet is, by weight, close to half oxygen. You just can't breathe it.

cards.headline: The element that joins almost everything
cards.body: Oxygen reacts with practically every other element, and that eagerness is why flames and bodies both need it. Burning usually combines a fuel with oxygen from the air, giving off heat and light. Remember Level 9's candle turning wax into carbon dioxide and water? Oxygen is the wax's partner in that change. Your cells use it too: they combine oxygen with food molecules to release energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
cards.callout: Priestley's candle and mouse were running on the same partner.

mascot.line: Even great chemists get one wrong. Lavoisier's just got printed on every periodic table.

cards.headline: Named for a mistake
cards.body: Carl Scheele discovered oxygen about 1772, and Priestley found it independently in 1774. But Antoine Lavoisier gave it its name: oxygène, from Greek words meaning acid former, because he believed every acid contained it. He was wrong. Chemists later found acids with no oxygen at all, such as hydrochloric acid. By then the name had stuck, and it's been stuck ever since.

title: Carbon
objective: After this level you can explain why carbon is the basis of life.
summary: Carbon is scarce in the crust yet forms more compounds than all other elements, because each atom bonds to four others, including carbon. Life is built mostly of carbon compounds.

cards.headline: A trace of Earth's rocks, and the builder of everything alive.
cards.body: Carbon is only a few hundredths of a percent of Earth's crust. Yet it forms more compounds than all the other elements combined, from plastic to you. How does one scarce element get so busy?

cards.fact: A carbon atom can bond to four other atoms at once, including other carbon atoms.
cards.context: Those links are strong, and because carbon can link to itself, it builds chains, branched chains and rings of many sizes and shapes. Here's an analogy: think of a building brick with four studs that snaps happily onto more bricks just like it. With a brick like that, you can build a line, a tree, a loop, or all three at once.

mascot.line: Sixty zeros. I tried to write them all down and ran out of scroll.

cards.headline: Ten million known, and counting
cards.body: Close to ten million carbon compounds are already known, and chemists estimate that the number of possible ones is 10^60: a 1 followed by 60 zeros. That's how carbon outbuilds all the other elements combined. Your T-shirt's fibers, the plastic in your pen, the soap by your sink, the medicine in your cabinet: all carbon compounds.

cards.headline: The element of life
cards.body: All living things on Earth are made mostly of carbon compounds. In organic molecules, carbon is the main element, bonded to hydrogen and to other carbon atoms. So Level 31's hydrogen, the universe's most common element, is carbon's constant companion inside you. Chemists call the study of these molecules organic chemistry, and it's why carbon earns its title: the element of life.

title: Diamond and Graphite
objective: After this level you can explain how carbon can form both diamond and pencil lead.
summary: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Diamond's atoms each bond to four others in 3D, making it very hard; graphite's sheets slide, so it marks paper.

cards.headline: Your pencil and a diamond ring are made of the same element.
cards.body: One is soft enough to smear across paper. The other is the hardest natural substance known. Both are pure carbon. The difference isn't what they're made of. It's how the atoms are arranged.

cards.fact: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon: two forms, called allotropes, of one element.
cards.context: They're carbon's two most common forms. Same atoms, different arrangement, completely different personalities. As an analogy, imagine one box of bricks built once into a solid block and once into a stack of loose sheets. The next two cards show the real arrangements.

cards.headline: Diamond: every atom locked in four ways
cards.body: In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four others, in a network that runs in all three dimensions. Remember Level 33's four bonds? Diamond uses all of them on more carbon, and that structure makes it the hardest known natural substance. Diamonds form more than 120 km down in Earth's mantle, where temperatures and pressures are immense, and volcanic eruptions carry them up.

mascot.line: So a diamond is forever mostly because it's in no hurry.

cards.headline: Graphite: sheets that slide
cards.body: In graphite, carbon atoms lie in flat sheets of linked hexagons, like chicken wire. The sheets hold together only weakly, so they slide apart easily: drag a pencil across paper and layers stay behind. Graphite also conducts electricity, which diamond does not. The twist: at room temperature graphite is the more stable form. A diamond just changes so slowly that it lasts indefinitely.

cards.headline: Why it's called pencil "lead"
cards.body: Pencil lead is graphite mixed with clay, and it contains no lead at all. When a pure graphite deposit was found at Borrowdale, England, in 1564, people thought it was a kind of lead. In 1779 Carl Scheele, the same chemist who found oxygen, showed it was carbon. The old name stuck anyway. The new one fits better: graphite comes from the Greek graphein, to write.

title: Iron
objective: After this level you can explain iron's role in steel and in your blood.
summary: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole and the most-used metal. A little carbon turns soft iron into steel. In your blood, iron sits in hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from your lungs.

cards.headline: The same element holds up bridges and carries oxygen in your blood.
cards.body: Iron is in the steel of skyscrapers and in every drop of your blood. How does one element manage both jobs?

cards.fact: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole: about 35 percent.
cards.context: Most of it is far out of reach, in the planet's core, which is made chiefly of iron. In the crust, iron comes fourth, at about 5 percent, after oxygen, silicon and aluminum. That's still plenty to go around: iron is the most-used and cheapest metal we have.

cards.headline: A pinch of carbon makes steel
cards.body: Pure iron is surprisingly soft. Add a little carbon, up to about 2 percent, and you get steel: far harder, and by far the most widely used material for building the world's infrastructure. Add more, 2 to 4 percent, and you get cast iron, which is brittle and weak when pulled. Level 33's carbon, in tiny amounts, turns a soft metal into the backbone of cities.
cards.callout: Iron + up to 2% carbon = steel

mascot.line: Same element in a bridge girder and in you. You're a little bit infrastructure.

cards.headline: The iron in your blood
cards.body: Most of the iron in your body sits in hemoglobin, the protein in your blood that carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Remember Level 32: your cells combine oxygen with food to release energy. That oxygen has to reach them somehow, and iron is part of the delivery system. No iron, no delivery.

title: Gold and Silver
objective: After this level you can explain why gold and silver were prized for money and jewelry.
summary: Gold barely reacts, so it never tarnishes and is found nearly pure. Some of the earliest coins used electrum, a natural gold-silver mix. Silver conducts best of all metals but tarnishes with sulfur.

cards.headline: Gold never tarnishes. That's worth a fortune.
cards.body: For well over two thousand years, people have trusted gold and silver with their wealth, as coins and as jewelry. Chemistry explains a lot of that trust, and why silver always seems to come second.

cards.fact: Gold doesn't corrode or tarnish: oxygen and sulfur leave it alone.
cards.context: It's one of the least reactive metals. Level 32's oxygen reacts with practically everything, and gold is one of the rare holdouts. That's why gold is usually found fairly pure in nature, as nuggets. It's also the most malleable element: one ounce can be hammered into a sheet of about 300 square feet. A metal that lasts and stretches that far makes a fine treasure.

cards.headline: The first coins had a chemistry problem
cards.body: Some of the earliest coins were struck in Lydia, in the second half of the 7th century BCE, from electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver. The catch: with two metals in varying amounts, it was hard to calculate what a coin was worth. So King Croesus replaced them with coins of highly pure gold and pure silver. Money got more trustworthy the moment its chemistry got simpler.

mascot.line: Silver wins every conductivity contest, then shows up to the photo looking tarnished.

cards.headline: Silver: the best conductor, with one weakness
cards.body: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals. Its weakness is sulfur: traces of sulfur compounds in the air tarnish it with a dark coating of silver sulfide. Gold ignores sulfur and oxygen alike. That's why silverware needs polishing and a gold ring doesn't.

title: Copper and Bronze
objective: After this level you can explain how bronze began an age of history.
summary: Copper was one of the first metals used. Mixed with tin it makes bronze, harder and easier to cast, the first metal widely used for tools and weapons: the Bronze Age.

cards.headline: Add a little tin to copper, and you get a metal that named an age.
cards.body: Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age. One of those names isn't a single element at all: bronze is a mix of copper and tin. How did a mixture of two metals change how people lived?

cards.fact: Copper was one of the first metals people used, about 10,000 years ago.
cards.context: Copper turns up in nature as a free metal, so Neolithic people could use lumps of it in place of stone, around 8000 BCE. It's still a star: copper is second only to Level 36's silver in conducting electricity, and electrical industries use most of the copper produced.

cards.headline: Bronze: copper plus tin
cards.body: Around 3500 BCE, metalworkers began deliberately mixing copper with tin. The result, bronze, is harder than copper, and it melts more readily, so it's easier to pour into molds. Modern bronze is typically about 88 percent copper and 12 percent tin. Push the tin up to 20–25 percent and you get bell metal, a bronze that rings when struck.
cards.callout: Copper + tin = bronze: harder, and easier to cast

mascot.line: Copper on its own: useful. Copper with the right partner: history-making.

cards.headline: An age named for a mixture
cards.body: Bronze became the first metal in widespread use for tools and weapons, and an era of history carries its name: the Bronze Age. Around 1000 BCE, the ability to heat and forge iron (Level 35) brought it to an end. And bronze has a sibling you met in Level 6: brass, a solid solution of copper and zinc. Copper, it turns out, makes a great mixer.

title: Aluminum
objective: After this level you can explain why aluminum was once more precious than gold.
summary: Aluminum is the crust's most common metal but never occurs as metal, so it once outvalued gold. In 1886 Hall and Heroult freed it with electricity, and its price collapsed.

cards.headline: An emperor's best guests ate with aluminum cutlery.
cards.body: Napoleon III's most important guests got aluminum; the rest made do with mere silver. Today the same metal turns up in cooking pots and airplanes. What changed?

cards.fact: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8 percent by weight.
cards.context: Only oxygen and silicon are more plentiful, and Level 35's iron comes after it. So why was it ever rare? Because aluminum is chemically active, it never occurs as a metal in nature. It's locked tight in compounds in rocks. Abundant everywhere, and for a long time out of reach.

cards.headline: Once more valuable than gold
cards.body: In the mid-1800s, aluminum was more valuable than gold. Only small amounts could be pried out of its compounds, at great cost. That's why an emperor showed off aluminum cutlery. It was a showpiece metal, and a remarkably light one: aluminum is only about one-third as dense as iron or copper.

mascot.line: A world-changing discovery, made partly in a woodshed. Never underestimate a shed.

cards.headline: 1886: electricity sets it free
cards.body: In 1886, Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Heroult in France independently cracked it: pass electricity through purified alumina, a compound of aluminum and oxygen, dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite. Hall worked partly in his family's woodshed. By 1891 aluminum cost less than $1 a pound. A treasure fit for an emperor became a metal for cooking pots.

title: Silicon
objective: After this level you can explain why silicon runs our computers.
summary: Silicon, the crust's second element, is locked with oxygen in rock and sand. A semiconductor tuned by doping, ultra-pure silicon becomes the transistor switches in chips.

cards.headline: The brain of your phone started out as the stuff of sand.
cards.body: Sand is full of silicon locked up with oxygen. Free that silicon, purify it to an extreme, and you have the material inside computer chips. What makes this element so right for the job?

cards.fact: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, after oxygen: more than a quarter by weight.
cards.context: Pure silicon is never found free in nature. It sits in practically all rocks, sand, clays and soils, combined with oxygen as silica, in minerals like quartz. Level 32's oxygen is nearly half the crust, so together these two make up most of the ground under your feet.

cards.headline: Not a metal, not an insulator: a semiconductor
cards.body: Metals like copper conduct electricity easily; insulators hardly at all. Silicon is a semiconductor, somewhere in between, and its conductivity can be tuned. Add about 10 boron atoms for every million silicon atoms, a process called doping, and it conducts a thousand times better. Sound familiar? It's Level 35's steel trick: a pinch of another element transforms the material.
cards.callout: 10 boron atoms per million: about 1,000 times more conductive

mascot.line: First remove nearly every impurity. Then add some back, very carefully. Chemists love a plot twist.

cards.headline: Why chips need absurdly pure silicon
cards.body: Doped silicon makes transistors, tiny switches that turn electric current on and off, and computer chips are built from them. Silicon has become by far the most widely used semiconductor, virtually replacing germanium. Because a few stray atoms change how silicon conducts, chip-makers start from extremely pure silicon: fewer than 1 stray atom per 10 billion. Then they add exactly the impurities they want.

title: Molecules
objective: After this level you can explain what a molecule is.
summary: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds, the smallest piece that is still the substance. Every water molecule has the same recipe: two hydrogens, one oxygen.

cards.headline: Halve a drop of water, again and again. When does it stop being water?
cards.body: No knife is that sharp, but chemists know the answer. There is a smallest piece of water that is still water, and it has a name.

cards.fact: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
cards.context: It's the smallest piece a pure substance can be split into and still be that substance. Remember Level 3? All matter is made of tiny particles: atoms, which can join into molecules. The water in your glass is a vast crowd of water molecules, and every single one of them is still water.

cards.headline: Split the molecule, lose the water
cards.body: A water molecule is built from hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Break it apart and you don't get tinier water. You get hydrogen and oxygen, two gases that behave nothing like the stuff you drink. So the molecule is the last stop: one step smaller, and the water is gone.

mascot.line: Water's recipe card has never once been edited. Very dependable, water.

cards.headline: A recipe that never changes
cards.body: Every water molecule holds exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Always. That fixed recipe is what makes water a compound rather than a mixture: Level 6's cookie can have more chips or fewer, but water can't have extra oxygen. Not every molecule mixes elements, though. Most of the oxygen and nitrogen in the air comes as molecules of two identical atoms, paired up.

title: Water
objective: After this level you can explain what makes the water molecule so special.
summary: Water is polar: oxygen pulls shared electrons harder. Hydrogen bonds between molecules make water boil at 100 °C, not about −80 °C, give it surface tension and hold ice's open lattice.

cards.headline: By the pattern of similar compounds, water should boil at about −80 °C.
cards.body: It boils at 100 °C instead. If water followed the pattern, the drink in your glass would be a gas at room temperature. The explanation is one lopsided little molecule.

cards.headline: A lopsided molecule
cards.body: Inside a water molecule, the atoms share electrons, but not fairly. Oxygen pulls harder, so its end of the molecule carries a slight negative charge, and the two hydrogen ends carry slight positive charges. The hydrogens sit at an angle of about 104.5°, not in a straight line, so the molecule has a negative side and a positive side. Chemists call that polar.
cards.callout: Polar: slightly negative at one end, slightly positive at the other

cards.headline: Molecules that cling
cards.body: The positive hydrogen end of one water molecule is drawn to the negative oxygen end of its neighbor. That pull between molecules is a hydrogen bond. Each one is much weaker than the bonds inside a molecule, but a glass of water is full of them. Remember Level 4? To boil, particles must break away from their neighbors. For water, that means breaking hydrogen bonds, which is why it boils at 100 °C, not −80 °C.

mascot.line: Next time a paper clip floats, thank the hydrogen bonds. Politely.

cards.headline: A skin on the pond
cards.body: All that clinging gives water's surface a kind of skin, called surface tension. It's strong enough for water striders to walk across a pond, and it can even float a steel paper clip.

cards.headline: Level 8's ice, explained
cards.body: Remember Level 8's floating ice? When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open lattice that holds them farther apart than in the liquid. Same mass, more space: ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. Icebergs bob on the sea because of a lopsided molecule.

title: Salt and Ionic Bonds
objective: After this level you can explain ionic bonds using table salt.
summary: Sodium gives an electron to chlorine; the opposite ions attract in an ionic bond. Salt is a grid of ions, not molecules. It melts at 801 °C, yet water pulls its ions apart.

cards.headline: Table salt is made from a soft metal and a poisonous gas.
cards.body: Sodium is a silvery metal that burns vigorously in air. Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that is very poisonous. Together they make the white crystals you sprinkle on fries. How does a dangerous pair become dinner?

cards.fact: An ionic bond is the attraction between two oppositely charged ions.
cards.context: Here's the trade. Each sodium atom hands one electron to a chlorine atom. Losing a negative electron leaves sodium positively charged; gaining one makes chlorine negatively charged. Atoms with a charge are called ions, and opposite charges attract. That grip between a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion is the ionic bond.

cards.headline: There's no such thing as a salt molecule
cards.body: Water comes in molecules. Salt doesn't. Its ions stack into a three-dimensional grid, and each one is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge. No ion belongs to just one partner. A grain of salt is one enormous, orderly team of ions, with no single molecule to point to.
cards.callout: Ionic compound: a grid of ions, not a crowd of molecules

mascot.line: Mystery from Level 9: solved. Those charged particles had names all along.

cards.headline: Tough to melt, easy to dissolve
cards.body: All those attractions make salt hard to melt: it holds out until 801 °C. Yet drop it in water and it falls apart. Level 42's polar water molecules surround the ions and pull sodium and chloride apart. Remember Level 9's gray area, where dissolved salt came apart into charged particles? These ions are those particles.

title: Covalent Bonds
objective: After this level you can explain how atoms share electrons.
summary: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Atoms can share one, two or three pairs; nitrogen's triple bond keeps it unreactive. Melting and boiling leave these bonds intact.

cards.headline: Salt's atoms trade electrons. Most molecules share them instead.
cards.body: Hydrogen gas, the nitrogen in the air, the water in your glass and every organic compound are held together not by a trade but by a share. So how do two atoms share an electron?

cards.fact: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms.
cards.context: In a hydrogen molecule, the two atoms share a pair of electrons that sits between them, and both hold on. Identical atoms share perfectly equally. Different atoms share unequally, which makes the bond polar: that's Level 42's lopsided water. Picture a tug-of-war over the pair (an analogy) that nobody ever wins outright.

mascot.line: Nitrogen: the great introvert of the atmosphere.

cards.headline: One, two or three pairs
cards.body: Atoms can share more than one pair. A hydrogen molecule has a single bond: one shared pair. Oxygen gas has a double bond: two pairs. Nitrogen gas has a triple bond, three pairs, and it's very strong. That's why nitrogen, about 78 percent of the air, is so unreactive. Every breath you take is mostly a gas that would rather be left alone.

cards.headline: Strong inside, loose outside
cards.body: Here's the twist. The bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the pulls between neighboring molecules are much weaker. So covalent substances usually melt and boil far lower than salt, and many are liquids or gases at room temperature. When ice melts or water boils (Level 4), the molecules just move apart; the bonds inside each one stay whole. Steam is still water.
cards.callout: Melting and boiling separate molecules; they don't break them
