title: Metallic Bonds
objective: After this level you can explain why metals conduct electricity and bend without breaking.
summary: In a metal, outer electrons roam as a sea around positive ions. Free electrons carry current, and a hammered metal's layers slide but stay bonded, while salt's shifted layers shatter.

cards.headline: Hit a metal bar with a hammer and it dents. Hit a salt crystal and it shatters.
cards.body: Both are held together by electrical attraction. So why does one bend and the other break? The answer is where the electrons go.

cards.headline: A sea of electrons
cards.body: In a metal, the atoms pack tightly and let their outermost electrons go. Those electrons don't belong to any one atom, or even any one pair. They wander through the whole piece, a sea of electrons around positive metal ions, and that shared sea holds the metal together: the metallic bond. Salt trades electrons, water shares them in pairs, and metals pool them.
cards.callout: Metallic bond: positive ions in a shared sea of electrons

cards.headline: Why electricity flows through metal
cards.body: Those free electrons are also why metals conduct electricity so well: the electrons can move, so a current can flow through the metal. Solid salt can't do this, because its ions are locked in place. Melt it or dissolve it, and the ions can move and carry a current.

mascot.line: The electron sea: the reason a dented pan is still a pan.

cards.headline: Bend, don't break
cards.body: Hammer a metal and its layers of ions slide past each other. The electron sea simply flows along, keeping everything bonded, so the metal flattens instead of cracking. Shift the layers of a salt crystal and ions of the same charge end up side by side. They repel, and the crystal shatters. Same hammer, opposite fates.

title: Crystals
objective: After this level you can explain how crystals form.
summary: A crystal's particles repeat a pattern in every direction: salt grains are cubes, snowflakes six-fold. Crystals grow from solutions, melts or vapor; slow growth makes giants like Naica's.

cards.headline: In 2000, miners in Mexico broke into a cave of crystals up to 11 meters long.
cards.body: How does anything grow that big? Start with what makes a crystal a crystal.

cards.fact: A crystal is a solid whose particles sit in a pattern that repeats in every direction.
cards.context: And the outside often shows the inside. Level 43's salt grid is cubic, so salt crystals are cubes. In ice, water molecules line up in a hexagonal pattern, which is why every snowflake has six-fold symmetry. Look closely at a snowflake and you're seeing the arrangement of its molecules, made big enough to catch on your sleeve.

cards.headline: Joining the pattern
cards.body: Crystals grow as particles join the pattern, each atom, ion or molecule settling into its place. They can grow from a solution, from a cooling melt, or straight from a vapor. You've met that last one already: Level 10's frost, water vapor turning straight into ice on a cold window, is crystals growing from a gas.

mascot.line: I once got impatient waiting for toast. Naica has me rethinking my life.

cards.headline: Slow and steady grows giants
cards.body: Speed matters. Crystals that form fast stay small; slow growth makes bigger ones. Naica's gypsum crystals grew in hot, mineral-rich water that stayed in a narrow, steady temperature range for many hundreds of thousands of years. With that much time, a crystal can grow to 11 meters. Patience, on a geological scale.

title: Polymers
objective: After this level you can explain long-chain molecules like plastic and DNA.
summary: A polymer is a giant molecule of repeating units. Polyethylene is ethylene linked into long chains. Nature makes polymers too, from cellulose to DNA, whose chain in one cell stretches 6 feet.

cards.headline: A shopping bag and the DNA in your cells are built the same way.
cards.body: Both are chains: enormously long chains of small pieces, linked end to end. Chemists call them polymers.

cards.fact: A polymer is a giant molecule built from many small repeating units, called monomers.
cards.context: The name gives it away: polymer means "of many parts." Picture a chain of paper clips (an analogy): each clip is a monomer, and the whole chain is one molecule. Level 41's water molecule has just three atoms. A polymer keeps adding links.

cards.headline: The plastic in your kitchen
cards.body: Polyethylene, the most widely used plastic in the world, is small ethylene molecules linked into long chains. It's the food wrap, the shopping bag and the detergent bottle. Remember Level 1's credit card? Polymers again. The length of the chains and the way they're arranged are what make plastics strong, light and flexible.

mascot.line: Six feet of chain in every cell, and still nobody can find the scissors.

cards.headline: Nature got there first
cards.body: Living things are full of polymers: cellulose in plant cell walls, starch, proteins, natural rubber and DNA. DNA's links come in four kinds, known as A, C, G and T, and the human genome is about 3 billion of them long. Unwind all the DNA in just one of your cells, lay it end to end, and it would stretch about 6 feet (about 1.8 meters). One cell, a person's height of chain.

title: Chemical Formulas
objective: After this level you can explain how a formula like H2O describes a molecule.
summary: A formula names atoms by symbol and counts them with subscripts: H2O, CO2, O2. One atom more makes a new substance (O3, H2O2). Salt's formula, NaCl, is a ratio of ions.

cards.headline: H2O is water. H2O2 is a bleach.
cards.body: One extra oxygen atom, and a drink becomes something used to bleach cloth and clean cuts. A chemical formula is a recipe where every character counts.

mascot.line: Tiny numbers, big consequences. Always read the small print.

cards.fact: A formula names each kind of atom with its symbol and counts it with a small number.
cards.context: H2O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom: Level 41's fixed recipe, written in three characters. No number means one. CO2, carbon dioxide, is one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. O2 is the oxygen gas from Level 41, two oxygen atoms paired up.

cards.headline: Change one number, change everything
cards.body: Formulas are unforgiving. O2 is the oxygen you breathe. Ozone, O3, has just one more oxygen atom, and it's a pale blue, irritating, toxic gas; high in the atmosphere, it absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet rays. H2O2, hydrogen peroxide, differs from water by one oxygen atom and is used as a bleach and an antiseptic. Same elements, different counts, different substances.
cards.callout: Same atoms, different counts: a different substance

cards.headline: Salt's formula is a ratio
cards.body: Salt is written NaCl, but Level 43 showed there's no salt molecule. So NaCl isn't a head count for one molecule. It's a ratio: one sodium ion for every chloride ion, all through the grid. Chemists call that a formula unit. The formula still gives you the recipe, even when there's no single dish.

title: Shapes of Molecules
objective: After this level you can explain why a molecule's shape matters.
summary: Electron pairs repel and spread out, setting a molecule's shape. Straight CO2 is nonpolar and bent water is polar; mirror-image carvones smell of spearmint and caraway.

cards.headline: One molecule smells of spearmint. Its mirror image smells of caraway.
cards.body: Same atoms, same bonds, same formula. The only difference is which way they're built, like your left hand and your right. For molecules, shape matters.

cards.headline: Electron pairs keep their distance
cards.body: Around a central atom, pairs of electrons repel each other, whether they're in bonds or not, so they spread as far apart as they can. That sets the shape. In methane, the four hydrogens around the carbon don't lie flat; they point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. Tie four balloons together at their knots and they settle into that same shape (an analogy).

cards.headline: Straight versus bent
cards.body: Carbon dioxide is straight: oxygen, carbon, oxygen in a line. Each bond is lopsided, but the two pull in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule isn't polar. Water is bent, at about 104.5°, because of the unshared electron pairs on its oxygen. Its lopsided bonds can't cancel, so water is polar. That bend is where Level 42's hydrogen bonds come from.
cards.callout: Straight CO2: pulls cancel. Bent H2O: they don't.

mascot.line: Your nose can tell left from right. Impressive, for a nose.

cards.headline: A handed nose
cards.body: Back to spearmint and caraway. Their carvone molecules are mirror images, like your hands. The odor receptors in your nose are handed too, so each form fits different receptors, the way a left hand fits a left glove but not a right one (an analogy). Different fit, different smell.

title: What a Reaction Is
objective: After this level you can explain reactants and products.
summary: A chemical reaction turns reactants into products by breaking bonds and rearranging the same atoms into new substances, which can behave completely differently from what you started with.

cards.headline: A campfire is a machine for making new stuff.
cards.body: Logs go in. Invisible gases, heat and a small heap of ash come out. The wood hasn't just changed shape; it has become different substances. Level 9 called that a chemical change. Chemists call the event itself a reaction.

cards.headline: Reactants in, products out
cards.body: The substances you start with are the reactants. The new substances a reaction makes are the products. For the campfire, the reactants are wood and oxygen from the air, and the products are carbon dioxide, water vapor and ash. Chemists write it with an arrow, reactants on the left and products on the right: wood + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water vapor + ash. Read the arrow as "turns into."

mascot.line: Same bricks, brand-new spaceship. Chemistry is a very tidy builder.

cards.headline: Same atoms, new partners
cards.body: Here's the trick: a reaction doesn't make new atoms or destroy old ones. It breaks the bonds holding the reactants together and reassembles the same atoms into new combinations, with every atom accounted for on both sides. Think of a toy-brick castle taken apart and rebuilt as a spaceship: every brick survives, only the arrangement changes.

cards.headline: New stuff, new personality
cards.body: Rearranging atoms can change everything about how a substance behaves. Hydrogen is a gas that burns. Burn it with oxygen and you get water, a compound with entirely different properties: it doesn't burn at all, and firefighters use it to put fires out. Same atoms, opposite job.

title: Nothing Is Lost
objective: After this level you can explain Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass.
summary: Mass is conserved in reactions. Lavoisier weighed tin heated in a sealed vessel; burning wood only seems to lose mass because gases escape, and metals gain mass as oxygen joins them.

cards.headline: A log weighs far more than its ashes. So where did the rest go?
cards.body: Burn a big log and you're left with a small, light heap of ash. It looks as if most of the wood simply vanished. This level is about why it didn't.

cards.fact: In a chemical reaction, mass is neither created nor destroyed.
cards.context: This is the law of conservation of mass, and it follows from Level 51. A reaction only rearranges atoms, so every atom you start with is still there at the end, and so is its mass. The products weigh exactly what the reactants weighed, even when some of them are invisible gases. If something seems lighter or heavier, matter has slipped in or out unseen.

mascot.line: When in doubt, weigh it. Then weigh it again.

cards.headline: The chemist who weighed everything
cards.body: Antoine Lavoisier, an 18th-century French chemist, made a habit of collecting and weighing every substance in his reactions. In one famous experiment he sealed tin inside a vessel with air, heated it, and weighed it all. The solids got heavier as some tin turned to powder. But the air inside got lighter by exactly the same amount. Nothing came in or out, so the total never changed.

cards.headline: Why the log fooled everyone
cards.body: Back to the campfire. The ash is light because most of the wood's mass left as carbon dioxide and water vapor, drifting off into the sky. Catch every wisp of that gas, add the ash, and it would weigh as much as the wood plus the oxygen it used. The opposite trick fools people too: when a metal combines with oxygen it gets heavier, because the oxygen's mass comes along.

title: Burning
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when something burns.
summary: Burning is a reaction of fuel with oxygen giving heat and light, mainly making carbon dioxide and water. A candle burns as wax vapor, and every fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat at once.

cards.headline: Fire isn't a thing. It's a reaction you can see.
cards.body: A flame looks like an object, but it is really an event: a chemical reaction giving off heat and light. So what exactly is reacting in there?

cards.headline: Fuel meets oxygen
cards.body: Burning, or combustion, is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that gives off heat and usually light. When the fuel is made of carbon and hydrogen, like candle wax, the main products are carbon dioxide and water. Starved of oxygen, burning can go wrong and also make carbon monoxide, a toxic gas with no color and no smell.
cards.callout: Plenty of oxygen: carbon dioxide and water. Too little: carbon monoxide.

mascot.line: The wick gets the credit. The vapor does the work.

cards.headline: What actually burns in a candle
cards.body: A candle has a neat secret. The flame's heat melts the wax and turns it into vapor, and it's the wax vapor, mixed with oxygen, that burns. So a flame is really a glowing cloud of reacting gas. Its heat keeps making more vapor, which keeps the flame going: a reaction that feeds itself.

cards.headline: The fire triangle
cards.body: Every fire needs three things at once: fuel, oxygen and heat. Firefighters call it the fire triangle, and it tells them how to win. Take away any one side and the fire goes out. Water cools it, stealing heat. Stop, drop and roll smothers flames, cutting off oxygen. A fireline cleared through a forest leaves the fire nothing to burn.

title: Rust
objective: After this level you can explain how and why iron rusts.
summary: Rust is iron oxide, formed when iron meets oxygen and water; salt speeds it up. Rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron, so it spreads; paint and zinc galvanizing keep it away.

cards.headline: The slowest reaction in your garden shed
cards.body: Leave an iron tool out in the rain and it slowly grows a reddish-brown crust. Nothing burned and nobody painted it. That crust is rust, and it's a chemical reaction happening in slow motion.

cards.headline: Iron plus oxygen plus water
cards.body: Rust is iron oxide: iron that has combined with oxygen. But oxygen alone isn't enough. Iron rusts when it meets oxygen and water together, which is why wet iron is in far more danger than dry iron. Salts speed the reaction up. And Level 52's law adds a twist: the oxygen's mass joins the iron, so rust weighs more than the iron it came from.

mascot.line: Rust: the guest who never leaves.

cards.headline: Rust doesn't know when to stop
cards.body: Some metals protect themselves. Copper, for example, grows a coating that shields the metal underneath. Rust doesn't. It flakes off, exposing fresh iron to the air, so the reaction keeps eating deeper, layer after layer. A rusty spot is never finished; it is just getting started.

cards.headline: How to stop rust
cards.body: Since rust needs oxygen and water, the fix is to keep them away. Paint puts a barrier over the iron. Galvanizing coats it with zinc, a metal that reacts with oxygen more readily than iron does, so the zinc corrodes instead and the iron underneath is spared. The zinc takes the hit so the iron doesn't have to.

title: Fast and Slow Reactions
objective: After this level you can explain what speeds reactions up or slows them down.
summary: Particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy. Heat, more surface and higher concentration make good collisions more frequent; cold slows reactions.

cards.headline: Same food, same kitchen. Why does the fridge buy you days?
cards.body: Leave food on the counter and it can spoil quickly. Put the same food in the fridge and it stays fresh for days. The spoiling reactions haven't changed; only their speed has. So what sets the speed of a reaction?

cards.headline: Reactions are collisions
cards.body: Particles can only react when they bump into each other. And not every bump counts: they have to meet the right way round and with enough energy. Chemists call that minimum energy the activation energy. Picture a crowded dance floor where only a solid, well-aimed high-five counts. Anything that makes good collisions more common speeds a reaction up.

cards.headline: Turn up the heat
cards.body: Remember Level 4? Heat makes particles move faster. Faster particles collide more often, and more of them hit hard enough to clear the activation energy. For many reactions, a rise of just 10 °C roughly doubles the rate. Now run it backward and you have your fridge: colder food, slower particles, fewer successful collisions, slower spoiling.

mascot.line: More surface, more collisions, more action. Chopping is chemistry.

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, faster reaction
cards.body: A solid can only react at its surface. Chop it into smaller pieces and far more surface is exposed. That's why a big log smolders, small sticks burn quickly and fine sawdust can burn explosively. Crowding in more reactant particles works too: a higher concentration usually means a faster reaction.

title: Catalysts
objective: After this level you can explain how catalysts speed up reactions without being used up.
summary: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by opening a route with a lower activation energy. Berzelius named catalysis in 1835; catalytic converters clean up car exhaust.

cards.headline: The helper that walks away unchanged
cards.body: Dilute hydrogen peroxide breaks down so slowly that it seems to do nothing. Poured onto an open wound, though, it breaks down fast and foams, releasing oxygen gas. What's different? Substances in the tissue are speeding the reaction up.

cards.fact: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
cards.context: When the reaction is over, the catalyst is still there, unchanged and ready to go again. The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius named the effect catalysis in 1835, from Greek words meaning "to loosen down."

mascot.line: Same start, same finish. Just a shortcut in the middle.

cards.headline: A tunnel through the mountain
cards.body: Remember Level 55's activation energy, the minimum energy a collision needs? A catalyst doesn't make particles hit harder. It opens a different route for the reaction, one with a lower activation energy. Picture two towns with a mountain between them: the catalyst is a tunnel. Far more travelers make it through, and the towns at each end stay exactly where they were. The reaction is the same, only faster.

cards.headline: A catalyst in your car's exhaust
cards.body: Modern cars clean their exhaust with a catalytic converter. Inside, metals such as platinum and rhodium help turn harmful gases into less harmful ones. Carbon monoxide and unburned fuel become carbon dioxide and water vapor. Nitrogen oxides become nitrogen and oxygen. And because a catalyst isn't used up, the same metals keep working as the car drives.

title: Energy In, Energy Out
objective: After this level you can explain reactions that give off heat and reactions that take it in.
summary: Exothermic changes release heat, like fire and rusting hand warmers; endothermic ones absorb it, like cold packs. The balance of bonds broken and made decides which.

cards.headline: One pouch warms your hands. Another cools a strained muscle.
cards.body: Neither one plugs in. Both run on chemistry. The difference is which way the heat flows: out of the chemicals and into you, or out of you and into the chemicals.

mascot.line: Warm hands, courtesy of rust. Who knew?

cards.headline: Exothermic: heat out
cards.body: A change that releases heat is exothermic. Every fire in Level 53 is exothermic. So is a disposable hand warmer, and here's the fun part: it is rusting. Unwrap it and oxygen reaches iron powder inside, which, with salt and water, turns into iron oxide and releases heat. It's Level 54's slow rust, sped up with fine powder for extra surface and salt for extra speed.

cards.headline: Endothermic: heat in
cards.body: A change that absorbs heat is endothermic. An instant cold pack holds water and a salt kept apart. When they are brought together, the process pulls heat in from its surroundings, including your sore muscle. The pack doesn't add cold; it takes heat away, and your skin reads that loss as cold.

cards.headline: Every reaction has an energy budget
cards.body: Level 51 said reactions break bonds and make new ones. That's the energy story too. Breaking a bond takes energy in; forming a bond gives energy out. If the new bonds release more than the old ones cost, the reaction is exothermic. If breaking costs more than making returns, it's endothermic.

title: Fireworks
objective: After this level you can explain how fireworks get their colors.
summary: Early fireworks were orange; colors came in the 1800s. Each comes from a metal whose heated electrons release light of its own color: strontium red, barium green, copper blue.

cards.headline: For centuries, fireworks came in one color.
cards.body: Fireworks go back more than 1,000 years, most likely to China. For centuries after that, they glowed only orange and gold, like sparks from a campfire. Then chemistry got hold of the palette.

cards.headline: Red, green, blue: pick a metal
cards.body: In the 1800s, chemists began adding newly made compounds and got reds, greens, blues and purples. Each color comes from a particular metal: strontium glows red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow. Mix two and you get blends, like copper and strontium for lavender. A firework's palette is really a list of elements.

mascot.line: Every color in the sky is an electron coming back down.

cards.headline: Why each metal has its own color
cards.body: The heat of the burning firework gives electrons in the metal atoms extra energy, bumping them up to higher energy levels. They don't stay there. As they drop back down, they give that energy off as light. The size of the drop sets the color, and each element has its own drops. That's why strontium reliably means red: it's a fingerprint written in light.

cards.headline: Blue, the hard one
cards.body: Blue is the most difficult firework color to produce. For a long time a "blue" firework was really an anemic bluish white. Only over recent decades have fireworks makers managed a true azure. So next time you watch a show, look for a deep, honest blue. It's the hardest trick in the sky.

title: Explosions
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a reaction explode.
summary: An explosion rapidly releases energy as expanding gas, often burning sped up. Deflagrations move slower than sound, detonations faster. Fine dust in air can explode.

cards.headline: In 2008, a sugar refinery exploded. The fuel was sugar.
cards.body: That year, a sugar dust explosion at a refinery in Port Wentworth, Georgia, killed 14 workers. Sugar is about as ordinary as a substance gets. How can it do that?

cards.headline: A reaction in a hurry
cards.body: An explosion is a rapid release of energy that produces a large volume of expanding gas in a very short time. Many explosions are simply burning sped up: when a combustion reaction accelerates far enough, a fire becomes an explosion. The hot gases have no time to drift away politely. They shove everything around them outward at once.

cards.headline: Fast, and faster still
cards.body: Chemists sort explosive reactions by speed. Low explosives, like gunpowder, burn extremely fast, but the reaction moves through them slower than sound. That's called deflagration. High explosives detonate: a shock wave races through the material faster than sound, setting it off as it goes. Same idea, a very different level of violence.

mascot.line: Same sugar, different shape. Surface area is not a small detail.

cards.headline: Why dust can explode
cards.body: Here's where Level 55 comes back. A log smolders, but sawdust can burn explosively, because smaller pieces expose more surface. Take that to the extreme: grind a burnable material into fine dust and hang it in the air, and every tiny grain is surrounded by oxygen. Sugar, flour, wood, coal, even metals such as aluminum can explode this way.

title: Checkpoint: Reactions
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in a chemical reaction and what controls its speed.
summary: Rusting and burning are both oxidation at different speeds. Rust, hand warmers, fire and explosions sit on one dial: rearranged atoms, conserved mass, and speed set by conditions.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one reaction, many speeds.
cards.body: A rusty gate, a hand warmer, a campfire and a dust explosion look like four different stories. Chemically, they are close relatives. Let's line them up.

cards.headline: Oxidation: combining with oxygen
cards.body: Rusting and burning belong to one family: oxidation. The word originally meant just what it sounds like, a substance combining with oxygen. The iron in rust and the fuel in a fire are both joining up with oxygen from the air. What separates them is speed. Rust creeps; fire races.

mascot.line: Same reaction family, four speeds. That is the whole chapter.

cards.headline: The chapter on one dial
cards.body: Picture a speed dial. At the slow end, iron rusts. Powder it and add salt, and the same reaction warms your hands. Turn the dial further with a fuel and plenty of heat, and oxidation races along as a flame. Push the reaction faster still and burning becomes an explosion. Temperature, surface area and catalysts are the knobs on that dial.

cards.headline: What never changes
cards.body: Whatever the speed, the rules hold. Reactants become products by rearranging the same atoms, so the mass is all still there, even when it floats away as gas. Fire and the hand warmer both give off heat: they are exothermic. And a catalyst can turn the dial without being used up.

title: Acids
objective: After this level you can explain what acids are, from lemons to stomach acid.
summary: Acids taste sour and hand off hydrogen ions in water. Strong acids like hydrochloric acid let go of nearly all; weak ones like vinegar's acetic acid hold on to most.

cards.headline: Lemons, vinegar and your stomach share one secret ingredient.
cards.body: A squeeze of lemon, a splash of vinegar, the juice churning in your stomach. One is a garnish, one is a dressing, and one is made by your own body. All three contain an acid. So what exactly makes something an acid?

cards.fact: The word acid comes from the Latin acidus: sour.
cards.context: Taste was chemistry's first acid test. Acids taste sour: citric acid gives lemons their pucker, acetic acid gives vinegar its bite, and your stomach makes hydrochloric acid. Chemists retired the taste test long ago, though. Tasting or touching chemicals is bad lab practice, so they identify acids with tests instead.

mascot.line: A whole family of tastes, explained by one tiny particle. I love it when chemistry tidies up.

cards.headline: The real secret: handing off hydrogen ions
cards.body: What truly makes an acid is what it does in water: it releases hydrogen ions, written H+. A hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron is just a bare proton, so chemists also call an acid a proton donor. Lemon juice, vinegar and stomach acid all do it. Different sources, same move.
cards.callout: Acid: a proton donor. It hands off hydrogen ions (H+) in water.

cards.headline: Strong or weak: how many let go
cards.body: Acids differ in how completely they hand off those ions. A strong acid, like hydrochloric acid, ionizes essentially completely in water: nearly every molecule lets go. A weak acid, like acetic acid, mostly holds on. In one textbook solution only about 1.3 percent of its molecules let go. Vinegar is a solution of about 5 percent acetic acid in water, and most of that acid is holding on tight.

title: Bases
objective: After this level you can explain what bases are, from soap to baking soda.
summary: Bases taste bitter and feel slippery: soap, ammonia, lye, baking soda. A base accepts hydrogen ions. Alkalis, named for plant ashes, are bases that dissolve in water.

cards.headline: The word alkali once meant a heap of plant ashes.
cards.body: It comes, by way of Medieval Latin, from the Arabic al-qili: the ashes of the saltwort plant. Something in those ashes was a base, the chemical partner of an acid. Meet the other half of this chapter.

cards.fact: Bases often taste bitter and feel slippery.
cards.context: That slippery feel belongs to a crowd you know. Soaps contain bases. Ammonia, a base, goes into household cleaners, and sodium hydroxide, better known as lye, is in drain cleaners. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is a mild base, gentle enough to use as an antacid. As with acids, chemists never taste-test: tasting or touching chemicals is bad lab practice.

cards.headline: Acid gives, base takes
cards.body: Level 61's acids hand off hydrogen ions. A base is the other side of the trade: it accepts them, which makes it a proton acceptor. Many bases, like sodium hydroxide, do it by releasing hydroxide ions, OH-, into water, and hydroxide snaps up hydrogen ions. Give and take: that's the whole partnership.
cards.callout: Base: a proton acceptor. Many release hydroxide ions (OH-).

mascot.line: From campfire ashes to soap to chemistry's vocabulary. Not bad for a pile of burnt plants.

cards.headline: Alkalis: bases that dissolve, and bite
cards.body: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, such as sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide. The name remembers where people first found them: alkali was leached out of the ashes of burned plants, and alkali reacting with fats or oils makes soap. Strong alkalis are caustic, too: they attack skin and other living tissue. Slippery, yes. Friendly, no.

title: The pH Scale
objective: After this level you can explain the pH scale.
summary: Sorensen gave acidity one number, pH, in 1909. It runs 0 to 14 with 7 neutral, and each step is tenfold: lime juice is about 1,000 times as acidic as coffee.

cards.headline: The pH scale was born in a beer company's laboratory.
cards.body: In 1909 the Danish chemist S.P.L. Sorensen ran the chemistry department at the Carlsberg Laboratory, backed by the brewery of the same name. He needed a simple way to say how acidic something was. His answer is a number you now meet everywhere: pH.

cards.headline: One number from 0 to 14
cards.body: Before Sorensen, there was no widely accepted way to say how acidic a solution was. pH fixed that. The scale usually runs from 0 to 14, and 7 is neutral: pure water. Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic. Lime juice sits around 2 and coffee around 5, while household ammonia is up near 12. One number tells you which side of the line you're on.

mascot.line: Three little steps, a thousandfold jump. The pH scale does not do small talk.

cards.headline: Each step is ten times
cards.body: Here's the twist: pH is not like a ruler. Each whole step is a tenfold change, so water at pH 5 is ten times more acidic than water at pH 6. Lime juice at about 2 is three steps below coffee at about 5, which makes it 10 x 10 x 10: about 1,000 times more acidic. Small numbers, big differences.
cards.callout: One pH step = ten times more (or less) acidic.

cards.headline: Why the numbers run backward
cards.body: Remember Level 61's hydrogen ions? pH is built from how many a solution holds, defined as the negative logarithm of their concentration. The minus sign is why the scale runs backward: the more hydrogen ions, the lower the pH. A low pH means lots of hydrogen ions, a high pH means few.

title: Neutralization
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when an acid meets a base.
summary: Acid meets base: hydrogen and hydroxide ions join into water, and the leftovers form a salt. Antacids are bases that neutralize some stomach acid.

cards.headline: A strong acid plus a caustic base can leave you with salt water.
cards.body: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid. Sodium hydroxide is lye, the caustic alkali from Level 62. When the two meet in matching amounts, what's left is sodium chloride, table salt, dissolved in water. How do two harsh chemicals cancel each other out?

cards.headline: Hydrogen meets hydroxide
cards.body: Neutralization is the acid-base partnership run to completion. Hydrogen ions from the acid meet hydroxide ions from the base, and each pair joins into a molecule of water: H+ plus OH- makes H2O. With hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, the leftover sodium and chloride ions make sodium chloride, table salt.
cards.callout: Acid + base → salt + water.

cards.headline: "Salt" is a whole family
cards.body: To a chemist, salt doesn't just mean the stuff in your shaker. A salt is any compound built from ions, a positive ion other than H+ and a negative ion other than OH-. Every acid-base neutralization makes a salt plus water. Table salt is just the family's most famous member.

cards.headline: Neutral, or close to it
cards.body: When a strong acid meets a strong base in matching amounts, the result is neutral: pH 7, the middle of Level 63's scale. Other pairings can leave the salt solution slightly acidic or slightly basic. Either way, something new has formed, a salt and water, which makes neutralization a chemical change.

mascot.line: Next time an antacid helps, you can thank a neutralization reaction by name.

cards.headline: Neutralization in your medicine cabinet
cards.body: Antacids are bases on purpose. Milk of magnesia, which is magnesium hydroxide, releases hydroxide ions that neutralize some of the hydrochloric acid in your stomach. Calcium carbonate antacids do the same job and give off carbon dioxide as they work.

title: Indicators
objective: After this level you can explain how red cabbage juice can test for acids.
summary: Indicators change color with pH: red cabbage runs from red to greenish-yellow, litmus turns red in acid and blue in base. Blue hydrangeas mean acidic soil.

cards.headline: A red cabbage can tell an acid from a base.
cards.body: Its purplish juice turns red in strong acids and greenish-yellow in strong bases. No batteries, no screen, no lab. So how does a vegetable run a chemistry test?

cards.fact: An indicator is a substance that changes color when it meets an acid or a base.
cards.context: The trick is in the molecule's shape. In pigments like the ones in red cabbage, a change in pH changes the molecule's structure, and a different structure shows a different color. So an indicator's color is a readout: Level 63's number, painted on.

mascot.line: Coleslaw with a secret talent. I will never look at a salad bar the same way.

cards.headline: Cabbage's rainbow
cards.body: Red cabbage gets its color from pigments called anthocyanins, and they're sensitive to pH. Very acidic solutions turn them red. Neutral ones leave them purplish. Mildly basic ones turn them blue to blue-green, and strongly basic ones greenish-yellow. One vegetable, a whole pH chart.

cards.headline: Litmus: the lichen test
cards.body: The classic lab indicator comes from lichens. Litmus is a mix of colored compounds from several lichen species that grow in the Netherlands. It turns red in acids and blue in bases, and it's the oldest and most commonly used acid-base indicator. Red means acid, blue means base: two colors, one answer.
cards.callout: Litmus: red in acid, blue in base.

cards.headline: A garden-sized pH test, with a twist
cards.body: Hydrangeas bloom blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil. But here the flower isn't acting as the indicator. Acidic soil makes aluminum more available to the roots, and aluminum reaching the flowers turns them blue. In alkaline soil, less aluminum gets through, and the blooms stay pink. The pH opens the gate; the aluminum paints.

title: Acid Rain
objective: After this level you can explain what causes acid rain.
summary: Normal rain is about pH 5.6; acid rain, from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, is more than ten times as acidic. US power plant SO2 fell 96 percent, 1990 to 2023.

cards.headline: In 1852 a chemist found acid falling from factory-town skies.
cards.body: The Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith studied rainwater near industrial cities in England and Scotland, and found acid rain. In 1872 his book Air and Rain laid it out. Where was the acid coming from?

cards.headline: All rain is a little sour
cards.body: Even clean rain isn't neutral. Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in it and forms weak carbonic acid, giving normal rain a pH of about 5.6. Acid rain usually measures between 4.2 and 4.4. That gap looks small, but on Level 63's tenfold scale it's more than one full step: acid rain is more than ten times as acidic as normal rain.

cards.headline: Where the extra acid comes from
cards.body: The culprits are sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. A little comes from volcanoes, but most comes from burning fossil fuels in power plants, vehicles and industry. In the air, these gases react with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form sulfuric and nitric acids. Then it all comes down as rain, snow, fog or even dry particles.

mascot.line: A statue losing its nose to the weather is chemistry working very, very slowly.

cards.headline: What it does on the ground
cards.body: Acid rain leaches aluminum out of soil and into lakes and streams, and strips away nutrients that trees need. At pH 5, most fish eggs can't hatch. It also eats at stone and metal, so statues and monuments slowly lose their carved detail.

cards.headline: A problem we largely cut
cards.body: The fix went after the source. The US Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 created the Acid Rain Program, the first national cap-and-trade program: power plants got a cap on sulfur dioxide and could trade allowances. Between 1990 and 2023, annual sulfur dioxide emissions from US power plants fell by 96 percent (EPA).

title: A More Acidic Ocean
objective: After this level you can explain how extra carbon dioxide affects the oceans.
summary: The ocean absorbs about 30 percent of released CO2, making carbonic acid; surface pH has dropped about 0.1. Shell builders struggle, and hatcheries fight back with a base.

cards.headline: The ocean is basic. It's just getting less so.
cards.body: Seawater sits above 7, on the basic side of Level 63's scale. But since the Industrial Revolution, its pH has been drifting down toward acid. The cause is carbon dioxide, and the ocean has been soaking it up.

cards.headline: The ocean drinks our carbon dioxide
cards.body: The ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere (NOAA, 2026). Dissolved in seawater, the gas forms carbonic acid, the same weak acid that makes Level 66's normal rain slightly sour. Carbonic acid breaks apart and releases hydrogen ions. And more hydrogen ions is exactly Level 61's recipe for acidity.

cards.fact: Since the Industrial Revolution, surface-ocean pH has dropped by about 0.1: roughly 30 percent more hydrogen ions (NOAA).
cards.context: A tenth of a pH unit sounds tiny, but the pH scale is logarithmic, so small steps are big changes. Seawater is still basic; it's just less basic. The IPCC's 2021 assessment calls it virtually certain that human carbon dioxide emissions are the main driver, and finds surface-ocean pH as low as in recent decades unusual in the last 2 million years.

mascot.line: A base to rescue baby oysters from acid. This chapter just keeps paying off.

cards.headline: Harder times for shell builders
cards.body: Those extra hydrogen ions react with carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells and coral skeletons, leaving fewer to go around. Oysters, clams, sea urchins and corals have to work harder to build calcium carbonate. In the US Pacific Northwest, oyster seed production plummeted by as much as 80 percent between 2005 and 2009. Hatcheries fought back by monitoring their seawater and adding sodium carbonate, a base, to balance its pH.

title: Batteries
objective: After this level you can explain how chemistry makes electricity in a battery.
summary: A battery splits a reaction: electrons flow from anode to cathode through your device while ions cross the electrolyte, sulfuric acid in cars, a base in alkaline cells.

cards.headline: Car batteries run on acid. Alkaline batteries run on a base.
cards.body: The lead-acid battery in a car holds sulfuric acid. An alkaline battery holds potassium hydroxide, one of Level 62's alkalis. Both names are chemistry clues. So what is an acid or a base doing inside a battery?

cards.headline: A reaction split in two
cards.body: A battery turns chemical energy straight into electrical energy by splitting a reaction between two ends. At one end, the anode, a substance gives up electrons. At the other, the cathode, a substance accepts them. The electrons' route between the two runs through the outside circuit: through your flashlight or phone. Recharging drives current backward and runs the reaction in reverse.

mascot.line: Electrons take the scenic route through your phone. Ions take the shortcut. Everybody gets home.

cards.headline: The electrolyte: a road for ions
cards.body: Between the anode and cathode sits the electrolyte, and that's where the acid or base lives. Electrons travel through the outside circuit, while charged ions move through the electrolyte inside the battery to balance them. The acid in a car battery isn't just a label: it's the ions' road.

cards.headline: The lemon battery, explained
cards.body: The classic lemon battery is Level 61 and this level at once. The lemon's acid reacts with a zinc strip and loosens electrons. Copper pulls electrons more strongly than zinc, so they flow through the wire toward the copper. The lemon juice is the electrolyte, and the energy comes from the metals reacting in its acid. The lemon itself isn't charged up.

title: Stomach Acid
objective: After this level you can explain how the stomach uses strong acid safely.
summary: Hydrochloric acid gives the stomach a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5. Bicarbonate mucus, tight junctions and a lining renewed every 3 to 6 days keep it from digesting itself.

cards.headline: Your stomach is full of hydrochloric acid. Why doesn't it dissolve itself?
cards.body: Special cells in your stomach lining make hydrochloric acid, the strong acid from Level 61. The lining it touches is living tissue. The stomach survives with layers of defense, and one of them is Level 64 in action.

cards.fact: Stomach contents have a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, thanks to hydrochloric acid.
cards.context: The acid comes from parietal cells in the stomach lining. On Level 63's scale that's firmly acidic, in the neighborhood of lime juice at about 2. The acid earns its keep: it kills much of the bacteria that arrive with your food and unfolds proteins so they're easier to digest.

mascot.line: An acid bath held off by a coat of mucus. Unglamorous, and absolutely brilliant.

cards.headline: Defense one: a blanket of base
cards.body: The stomach wall is covered in a thick coat of mucus rich in bicarbonate, a base. The mucus is a physical barrier, and its bicarbonate neutralizes acid that works its way in. Across the layer, the pH climbs: the stomach contents can be as acidic as pH 2 to 3 while the cells of the lining sit near neutral. Neutralization, on duty around the clock.

cards.headline: Defenses two and three: tight seams, fast repairs
cards.body: The cells of the lining meet at tight junctions, sealing the seams so gastric juice can't seep into the tissue beneath. And the surface lining is completely replaced every 3 to 6 days, so the lining is always fresh. Heartburn shows acid out of place: it's the painful burning you feel when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus, the tube from mouth to stomach.

title: Checkpoint: Acids and Bases
objective: After this level you can explain acids, bases and the pH scale with everyday examples.
summary: Water is amphiprotic: equal hydronium and hydroxide make pure water pH 7 at 25 °C. One day holds the whole chapter, from lemon water to a slowly acidifying sea.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: water is an acid. It's also a base.
cards.body: Every acid and base in this chapter did its work in water. Water can play both parts itself, and that explains why pure water sits right at 7. Then step back and find the whole chapter in one ordinary day.

cards.headline: Water trades with itself
cards.body: Water can hand off a hydrogen ion like an acid or accept one like a base, so chemists call it amphiprotic. In liquid water, a very small fraction of molecules actually trade: one gives a hydrogen ion to another. Each trade makes one hydronium ion, the acid side, and one hydroxide ion, the base side. Equal numbers of each: that's what neutral means.

mascot.line: Water, quietly refereeing every acid-base match in the chapter. Take a bow, water.

cards.headline: Why pure water is 7
cards.body: At 25 °C, pure water holds just one ten-millionth of a mole of each ion per liter, and on the pH scale that works out to exactly 7. Add an acid and hydronium outnumbers hydroxide: the pH falls. Add a base and hydroxide wins: the pH rises. Every number on Level 63's scale is a report on that tug-of-war.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one day
cards.body: Lemon in your morning water: citric acid, sour. Soap at the sink: a base, slippery. Lunch meets hydrochloric acid in your stomach, while bicarbonate mucus neutralizes what reaches the lining. Outside, rain falls slightly acidic from carbon dioxide, more so downwind of sulfur dioxide. And the sea, still basic, turns a little of our carbon dioxide into carbonic acid and drifts toward 7.

title: The Chemistry of Life
objective: After this level you can name the elements that living things are mostly made of.
summary: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96 percent of your mass. Oxygen leads by weight because of your water; hydrogen leads if you count atoms.

cards.headline: By mass, you are about 65 percent oxygen.
cards.body: Not the gas in your lungs: oxygen atoms built into you. Chemistry has plenty of elements on offer, but life is a picky eater. Which ones does it actually use?

cards.fact: Four elements make up about 96 percent of your body's mass: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen.
cards.context: By mass you're about 65 percent oxygen, 18 percent carbon, 10 percent hydrogen and 3 percent nitrogen. Every other element in you shares the last few percent. And it isn't just you: all four are common to every living organism, from an oak tree to a single bacterium.

mascot.line: Very organized. Mostly. Let's not talk about the sock drawer.

cards.headline: Why oxygen wins the weigh-in
cards.body: Up to 60 percent of an adult body is water, and each water molecule is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So a lot of your oxygen is sloshing around in your water. The oxygen atom is also far heavier than its two hydrogen partners. Put those together and oxygen piles up most of your mass. You're less a bag of bones than a very organized bag of water.

cards.headline: Count atoms instead, and hydrogen wins
cards.body: Weighing isn't the only way to rank. Count atoms one by one and hydrogen is the most common element in your body: more than 60 percent of your atoms are hydrogen. They're just so light that all of them together add up to only about a tenth of your mass. Same body, two rankings: oxygen by weight, hydrogen by headcount.

title: Sugars and Starches
objective: After this level you can explain carbohydrates as the body's fuel.
summary: Carbohydrates are carbon plus the parts of water. Glucose fuels your cells; plants store it as starch, you store it as glycogen, and cellulose is glucose you can't digest.

cards.headline: A baked potato and a cotton T-shirt are made of the same sugar.
cards.body: Both are chains of glucose. You can digest one of them, and it isn't the shirt. So what's the difference?

cards.fact: Carbohydrates are carbon plus the parts of water, which is exactly what the name says.
cards.context: Their general formula is (CH2O)n: "carbo" for carbon, "hydrate" for water. The family star is glucose, C6H12O6, built from three of Level 71's big four elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Glucose is an important energy source for your body. Your cells release its energy through cellular respiration, the story of Level 76.

cards.headline: Starch: glucose in storage
cards.body: Plants make more glucose than they need right away, so they link the extra into long chains called starch and tuck it away. A potato is a starch warehouse; so are grains of wheat, corn and rice. You store glucose too, as a chain called glycogen, kept mostly in the liver and muscles. It's the same trick: sugar packed into a pantry for later.

mascot.line: So technically your T-shirt is a snack. Just not for you. Or anyone without a very special gut.

cards.headline: Cellulose: the glucose you can't eat
cards.body: Cellulose is glucose too, but its units are linked a different way, and your digestive enzymes can't break those links. Cotton is about 90 percent cellulose and wood about 50 percent, which is why neither counts as lunch. Cows manage grass only with help from microbes in their gut. Same bricks, different mortar, completely different menu.

title: Proteins
objective: After this level you can explain proteins as chains of amino acids.
summary: Proteins are chains of hundreds or thousands of amino acids from 20 types. The order sets the fold, the fold sets the job, and heat can wreck the fold for good.

cards.headline: Your hair and an egg white are built from the same 20 parts.
cards.body: One is tough enough to braid. The other slides off a spoon. The parts are the same; the order is different. How much can order really change?

cards.fact: Proteins are chains of amino acids: hundreds or thousands long, drawn from 20 types.
cards.context: Think of the 20 amino acids as an alphabet and each protein as a very long word (an analogy, but a good one). With 20 letters and hundreds of positions, the possible words outnumber anything you could ever write down. Your genes spell out the exact order for each protein. One more detail: every amino acid carries nitrogen, in its amino group.

cards.headline: The shape is the job
cards.body: A protein chain doesn't stay a floppy string. Its sequence makes it fold into a particular 3D shape, and that shape decides what it does. Keratin forms tough strands in your hair and nails. Other proteins carry substances around your body, and many are enzymes that run your chemical reactions. Same alphabet, wildly different careers.

mascot.line: I tried un-frying one once. Breakfast was late that day.

cards.headline: Break the shape, break the protein
cards.body: Heat, a change in acidity or some chemicals can permanently scramble a protein's shape. Chemists call it denaturation, and you've watched it happen. In a hot pan, the albumin in egg white unfolds, and the clear, runny white turns white and firm. Cool it down as long as you like: nobody has ever un-fried an egg.

title: Fats
objective: After this level you can explain what fats are and why the body needs them.
summary: A fat is glycerol plus three fatty acids, and it won't dissolve in water. Straight chains make solid butter, kinked ones make liquid oil, and fat stores the most energy per gram.

cards.headline: Butter and olive oil are built the same way. One has kinks.
cards.body: That tiny difference in shape decides whether a fat sits solid on your counter or pours. First, though: what is a fat?

cards.headline: Glycerol plus three tails
cards.body: A fat molecule, or triglyceride, is a small molecule called glycerol with three long fatty acid tails attached. Fats are nonpolar, so they don't dissolve in water. That's why the oil in Italian dressing, Level 6's heterogeneous mixture, always drifts back apart from the rest no matter how hard you shake.

cards.headline: Straight tails stack. Kinked tails don't.
cards.body: In a saturated fat, the tails have only single bonds and run straight, so they pack tightly, like pencils in a box. That's why butter is solid at room temperature. In an unsaturated fat, double bonds put kinks in the tails, and kinked tails can't pack neatly. Olive oil stays liquid.
cards.callout: Straight tails: solid. Kinked tails: liquid.

cards.headline: Why your body keeps fat around
cards.body: A gram of fat holds 9 calories of energy, more than twice the 4 in a gram of carbohydrate or protein. That makes it the body's long-term energy store. Fat also insulates, forms part of every cell membrane, and helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, which dissolve in fat rather than water.

title: Photosynthesis
objective: After this level you can explain how plants make sugar from light, water and air.
summary: Van Helmont's willow gained 164 pounds but its soil barely changed. Plants build themselves from carbon dioxide and water, powered by light, and give off oxygen from split water.

cards.headline: A tree is built mostly out of thin air.
cards.body: Not soil. It took centuries to work that out, and the first careful experiment got the answer wrong.

cards.headline: The willow in the pot
cards.body: In the 1600s, Jan Baptista van Helmont planted a 5-pound willow in 200 pounds of soil and gave it only water for five years. The tree grew to 169 pounds. The soil lost about 2 ounces. So 164 pounds of tree had come from somewhere, and it clearly wasn't the dirt. Van Helmont concluded it came from the water alone. He never thought to suspect the air.

cards.fact: Six carbon dioxide + six water + light makes one glucose + six oxygen.
cards.context: That's photosynthesis, powered by light captured by chlorophyll. The glucose's carbon comes straight from carbon dioxide in the air, and that carbon makes up most of what a plant builds itself from. Van Helmont was half right: water is an ingredient. The rest of his willow was, mostly, air.

mascot.line: Water in, air out. Plants are the best recycling program on the planet.

cards.headline: The oxygen comes from the water
cards.body: Here's a twist: the oxygen a plant gives off doesn't come from the carbon dioxide. It comes from splitting water. In 1941, scientists proved it by tagging the water with a heavier kind of oxygen, oxygen-18, and finding that tag in the oxygen gas given off. So the oxygen a plant releases was once part of a water molecule.

title: Respiration
objective: After this level you can explain how cells release energy from food.
summary: Cells combine glucose with oxygen in their mitochondria, making carbon dioxide and water and capturing the energy in ATP, step by step. It's photosynthesis run in reverse.

cards.headline: Every breath out carries away a little of your breakfast.
cards.body: The carbon in the carbon dioxide you exhale was, not long ago, part of your food. How did it get from your plate to your breath?

cards.fact: Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.
cards.context: In symbols, C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O. It happens inside your cells, in tiny compartments called mitochondria, which use oxygen and give off carbon dioxide as waste. Breathing is just the delivery service: your lungs bring the oxygen in and carry the carbon dioxide, and your breakfast's carbon, back out.

cards.headline: Photosynthesis, run backward
cards.body: Put this next to Level 75's equation. Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Respiration turns glucose and oxygen back into carbon dioxide and water. Each one's products are the other's ingredients. The plant packs the Sun's energy into sugar; your cells unpack it.

mascot.line: Exact change only. Cells are very strict about this.

cards.headline: Small change, not a bonfire
cards.body: Your cells don't release a sugar's energy all at once. They take it apart in small steps instead of a single destructive burst, capturing the energy as they go in a molecule called ATP. ATP is often called the cell's energy currency: like breaking a big bill into coins (an analogy), it lets every part of the cell pay for exactly what it needs.

title: Enzymes
objective: After this level you can explain how enzymes speed up reactions in the body.
summary: Enzymes are protein catalysts: they speed reactions without being used up. A substrate fits their active site, and too much heat or extreme pH ruins that fit.

cards.headline: Chew plain rice long enough and it starts to taste sweet.
cards.body: Nobody added sugar. Something in your mouth is taking Level 72's starch apart into sugar, right on your tongue. Meet the enzyme.

cards.fact: Enzymes are the catalysts of life: they speed up reactions without being used up.
cards.context: An enzyme lowers the activation energy, the push a reaction needs to get started. Almost all enzymes are proteins, and each comes out of a reaction unchanged, ready to go again. The one in your rice is amylase, found in saliva. It breaks tasteless starch into sugars, including glucose, which your taste buds notice as sweetness.

cards.headline: A fit, not a force
cards.body: The molecule an enzyme works on is its substrate, and it binds in a pocket called the active site. The fit is so close that each enzyme is specific to its substrates. In 1894, Emil Fischer compared it to a lock and key. In 1958, Daniel Koshland refined the picture with induced fit: the active site reshapes as the substrate binds, more hand-in-glove than key-in-lock.

mascot.line: No fit, no reaction. Enzymes are wonderfully picky.

cards.headline: Too hot to work
cards.body: Remember Level 73's fried egg? Enzymes are proteins, so they share the weakness. High temperatures and extreme pH can denature an enzyme, changing its shape. Once the active site loses its shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme stops working. For an enzyme, shape isn't just important. It's everything.

title: Designing Medicines
objective: After this level you can explain how chemists design new medicines.
summary: Aspirin grew from willow bark: chemists isolated salicin, made gentler acetylsalicylic acid, and later learned how it works. Today drugs can be designed to fit an enzyme, then tested in phases.

cards.headline: More than 2,000 years ago, people used willow bark as medicine.
cards.body: Chinese and Greek healers both did. Today its descendant comes in a tablet. The road between the two shows how chemists design medicines.

cards.headline: Find it, then fix it
cards.body: In 1828, Johann Büchner pulled the active substance out of willow and named it salicin. Salicylic acid, made from it, eased pain but often irritated the stomach. At the Bayer company, Arthur Eichengrün set chemist Felix Hoffmann the task of making a better version, and in 1897 Hoffmann made acetylsalicylic acid, gentler on the stomach. That's aspirin: nature's molecule, tweaked by chemists.

cards.headline: Then, finally, understand it
cards.body: Here's the humbling part: aspirin was sold for decades before anyone knew how it worked. In 1971, John Vane showed that it blocks the body's making of prostaglandins, substances involved in pain, fever and inflammation. The work shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.

cards.headline: Designing to fit
cards.body: Modern chemists can start from the target instead. For HIV, knowing the crystal structure of a key HIV enzyme, its protease, was critical: chemists designed molecules to fit into it and jam it. The first of these drugs entered clinical use in 1995, one of the great success stories of structure-based drug design.

cards.headline: Then test, carefully
cards.body: A promising molecule then faces people in phases. Phase 1, with 20 to 100 volunteers, studies safety and dosage. Phases 2 and 3, with up to several hundred and then 300 to 3,000 people, test whether it works and watch for side effects.

title: The Dose Makes the Poison
objective: After this level you can explain why almost anything is harmful in a large enough dose.
summary: Paracelsus taught that the dose decides whether something is a poison; even water can be poisonous in excess. Foxglove shows the flip side: a toxic plant became a medicine in small doses.

cards.headline: Which is poisonous: a deadly plant, or a glass of water?
cards.body: Trick question. Either can be, and either can be harmless. What decides it was spelled out nearly five centuries ago.

cards.fact: "All things are poison and nothing is without poison. Solely the dose determines that a thing is not a poison."
cards.context: So wrote Paracelsus (1493 to 1541), a German-Swiss physician. He introduced the concept of dose and studied poisons by experiment. His idea is usually shortened to "the dose makes the poison," and it's still at the heart of toxicology, the science of poisons: how much of a substance you're exposed to matters enormously.

mascot.line: Half a question gets you half an answer. Chemists always ask: how much?

cards.headline: Even water
cards.body: Take the most harmless substance you can think of: water. By the dose concept, even water is poisonous if far too much of it is taken in. So "poison" isn't really a kind of substance. It's a substance plus an amount. Asking whether something is toxic, without asking how much, is only half a question.
cards.callout: Poison = substance + amount

cards.headline: Poison or medicine? Same plant.
cards.body: Foxglove is the flip side. In 1785, William Withering published a study showing that small, nontoxic doses of foxglove leaf treated dropsy, the swelling that came with heart failure. He also described the signs of digitalis poisoning, because a larger dose harms. Drugs containing digitalis, foxglove's active compound, are still prescribed today. One plant, two fates, decided by the dose.

objective: After this level you can explain how chemistry powers living things.
summary: Plants respire too: they have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. Follow one carbon atom from the air into a leaf, a potato, your mouth, your cells and back out on your breath.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: plants breathe out carbon dioxide too.
cards.body: Plants make sugar, you burn it. A neat division of labor? Not quite. Then follow one carbon atom through the whole chapter.

mascot.line: Chef and diner at once. Plants really have it figured out.

cards.headline: Plants respire too
cards.body: You might think plants only photosynthesize. Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. The chloroplasts make sugar from light; the mitochondria then burn some of that sugar in cellular respiration, making ATP, just as yours do. A plant is both the chef and a diner at its own restaurant.

You eat the potato; amylase starts breaking the starch into sugar. Your cells respire the glucose in their mitochondria, and the carbon rides out on your breath as carbon dioxide, ready for the next leaf.

title: Kitchen Chemistry
objective: After this level you can explain cooking as a series of chemical reactions.
summary: Heated sugars react with amino acids (the Maillard reaction) to brown food; sugar alone caramelizes. A wet surface stays near 100 °C, so browning waits for it to dry.

cards.headline: Toast is bread that went through a chemical reaction.
cards.body: Put pale bread in the toaster and it comes out brown, crisp and smelling wonderful. Nothing was added but heat. That new color and flavor are new substances, made right there in the slot. So what made them?

mascot.line: Chemistry you can eat. Easily the most popular kind of homework.

cards.headline: The Maillard reaction
cards.body: When food gets hot, its sugars react with the amino acids that make up its proteins. This is the Maillard reaction, named after the French scientist Louis-Camille Maillard, who first described it. It browns the food and builds new flavors and aromas: bread crust, seared meat, fried foods, roasted coffee. Every golden crust is a chemistry experiment you get to eat.

cards.headline: Caramel: sugar on its own
cards.body: Heat plain sugar, with no protein at all, and it browns anyway. That's caramelization: the heat breaks sugar down into new compounds with a brown color and new flavors. So a steak and a pan of caramel both brown, by two different reactions. Both are Level 9's chemical changes: new substances form, and they're hard to reverse. There's no un-toasting your toast.

cards.headline: Why wet meat won't brown
cards.body: Here's the catch cooks know well. While food is very wet, its surface can't get hotter than water's boiling point, 100 °C at sea level, as Level 4 showed. The heat goes into boiling the water off, not into raising the temperature. Only once the surface dries can it get hot enough for the Maillard reaction to take off. Patting meat dry isn't fussiness. It's chemistry.

title: Why Bread Rises
objective: After this level you can explain how yeast and baking soda make dough rise.
summary: Yeast ferments sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol; gluten traps the gas and the oven expands it. Baking soda and baking powder make the same gas without yeast.

cards.headline: The holes in your bread were blown by yeast.
cards.body: Slice a loaf and look at the crumb, full of little holes. Each one was a bubble of gas. In yeast bread, that gas came from tiny yeast cells having lunch.

cards.headline: Fermentation: yeast's lunch
cards.body: Yeast feeds on the sugars in dough and turns them into two things: carbon dioxide gas and alcohol (ethanol). This is fermentation. The gas is the part bakers want. As the yeast works, bubbles of carbon dioxide build up and the dough slowly rises. Every hole in your sandwich started as a yeast burp.

cards.headline: Gluten: the balloon skin
cards.body: Gas escapes easily unless something holds it. In wheat dough, that something is gluten, a stretchy network of proteins that traps the bubbles, so the dough expands instead of leaking. Remember Level 2's balloon: it grows because gas is matter and takes up space. Think of dough as a sponge of tiny balloons, each one filled with carbon dioxide.

cards.headline: The oven's last push
cards.body: In the hot oven, the trapped gas expands and the dough rises one more time. Then the heat kills the yeast, and most of the alcohol evaporates. The yeast made alcohol all along; the oven just sends most of it off into the air.

cards.headline: No yeast? Use baking soda
cards.body: You can get the gas without yeast. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) releases carbon dioxide when it's moistened and heated, and much more when the batter has an acidic ingredient such as honey, molasses or cocoa. Baking powder packs sodium bicarbonate together with its own acids, so it brings its own partner. Same gas, no yeast required.

title: How Soap Works
objective: After this level you can explain how soap lifts away grease.
summary: Oil and water don't mix, so water alone can't lift grease. A soap molecule has a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail; soap wraps grease in micelles that rinse away. Soap itself is made from fats.

cards.headline: Water alone can't get grease off a pan.
cards.body: Rinse a greasy pan and the water runs right over the grease. Oil and water don't mix; together they make a heterogeneous mixture, like Level 6's Italian salad dressing. Add a squirt of soap and the grease lets go. What does soap know that water doesn't?

cards.headline: A molecule with two ends
cards.body: Each soap molecule has two very different ends. Its head is attracted to water. Its long tail is attracted to oil and grease, and avoids water. So one soap molecule can hold on to both at once, the one thing water can't do on its own. It's a go-between with a foot in each world.

mascot.line: Tails in the grease, heads in the water. Everybody gets the seat they like.

cards.headline: Micelles: grease, gift-wrapped
cards.body: In soapy water, the tails dig into a grease droplet while the heads stay out in the water. Soap molecules surround the grease and form tiny clusters called micelles: grease locked inside, water-loving heads facing out.

cards.headline: Down the drain
cards.body: Now the rinse water has something to hold on to: the heads on the outside of each micelle. The clusters stay suspended in the water, and the rinse carries them away, grease and all. Water never learned to dissolve grease. Soap just wrapped it up so water could carry it.

cards.headline: Soap starts as fat
cards.body: The twist: soap itself is made from fats and oils. Reacting a fat or oil, such as tallow or vegetable oil, with a strong alkali turns it into soap, a reaction called saponification. The grease fighter began life as grease.

title: Cleaning Safely
objective: After this level you can explain why some cleaners must never be mixed.
summary: Bleach plus ammonia makes toxic chloramines; bleach plus acids like vinegar releases chlorine gas. Health agencies say never mix bleach, ventilate, and get fresh air after exposure.

cards.headline: Two cleaners that are safe alone can be dangerous together.
cards.body: Picture the cabinet under a sink: bleach, glass cleaner, a bottle of vinegar. The CDC's rule about them is blunt: never mix bleach with any other cleaner. The reason is a chemical change you already know how to spot.

cards.headline: Bleach plus ammonia
cards.body: Household bleach is sodium hypochlorite dissolved in water. Mix it with ammonia, found in some glass cleaners, and toxic gases called chloramines form. That's Level 9's chemical change: at least one new substance appears. This time the new substance is a gas, and it goes straight into the air you breathe.

cards.headline: Bleach plus acid
cards.body: Bleach mixed with acidic products releases chlorine gas. The acids hide in plain sight: vinegar, some toilet bowl cleaners, rust removers. Chlorine and chloramine gases irritate the eyes, nose and throat and cause coughing and trouble breathing. Higher exposures can damage the lungs.
cards.callout: Never mix bleach with ammonia or with acids

cards.headline: The second chemical isn't always in a bottle
cards.body: Urine contains ammonia. That's why Washington State's health department warns people to take care using bleach on litter boxes, diaper pails and toilets. A dangerous mix can happen with only one bottle in your hand.

mascot.line: One bottle at a time, window open. Some experiments are best left on the screen.

cards.headline: The habits that keep cleaning boring
cards.body: The CDC's advice is simple: never mix bleach with any other cleaner, keep the room well ventilated, and follow the label. If someone does breathe fumes from a mix, Poison Control says to leave the area right away for fresh air and call a poison center (1-800-222-1222 in the US). In cleaning, boring chemistry is the best chemistry.

title: Dyes and Colors
objective: After this level you can explain how dyes give cloth its color.
summary: Dyes absorb some colors of light and reflect the rest; mordants help some stay put. Dyes came from plants and snails until Perkin's 1856 mauve, the first synthetic dye sold.

cards.headline: In 1856, a teenager went looking for a medicine and found purple.
cards.body: William Henry Perkin was 18 and trying to make quinine, a malaria drug, from chemicals taken from coal tar. The medicine never appeared. A purple dye did: mauve, the first synthetic dye ever sold.

cards.headline: Before Perkin: plants and snails
cards.body: Until then, dyes came from plants and animals. Blue indigo came from plant leaves. Red came from the roots of the madder plant. Tyrian purple came from the glands of a sea snail. Purple, in other words, came from snail glands. Try scaling that up.

cards.headline: How a dye makes color
cards.body: A dye gives cloth a color that isn't easily changed by washing, heat or light. The color itself is about light. An object's color depends on which colors of light it absorbs and which it reflects. A red shirt reflects red light and absorbs the rest; black cloth absorbs all colors. What you see is the leftovers.

cards.headline: Making color stick
cards.body: A color that washes out is no use. Some dyes need a helper called a mordant, a metal salt that the fiber takes up. It reacts with the dye to make a less soluble form, held fast to the fabric. The word comes from the Latin mordere, to bite. The mordant gives the dye teeth.

cards.headline: Color from a flask
cards.body: Mauve came from a flask, not a snail. Perkin patented it in 1856, at 18, and it became the first commercialized synthetic dye: color made from coal-tar chemicals instead of harvested from plants and animals. A failed malaria medicine turned into a new way to make color.

title: How Smells Travel
objective: After this level you can explain how smell molecules reach your nose.
summary: Smelling is detecting airborne chemicals, so only volatile substances have a smell. Warmth frees more molecules, and diffusion spreads them in a slow zigzag because they keep colliding.

cards.headline: You can smell a pizza before you see it.
cards.body: The delivery box is still closed in the hallway, yet the smell is already in the room. Something real traveled from the pizza to your nose: molecules. Smell is the detection of chemicals carried in the air.

cards.headline: Only escapees have a smell
cards.body: If smelling means catching chemicals from the air, a substance can only have a smell if some of its molecules get into the air. Odor molecules are volatile: they vaporize readily. Anything you can smell right now is quietly sending bits of itself your way.

cards.headline: Warmth launches more molecules
cards.body: Remember Level 4: heating makes particles move faster. As a liquid warms, more of its molecules have enough energy to escape into the air. So a steaming bowl of soup sends more smell molecules into the room than the same soup straight from the fridge.

mascot.line: Imagine crossing a crowded party by bumping into every guest. That's a smell molecule's evening.

cards.headline: Fast molecules, slow journey
cards.body: Gas molecules zip along at hundreds of meters per second. So why does a smell take time to cross a room? Each molecule keeps colliding with other molecules and bouncing off in a new direction. The overall spreading, from where molecules are crowded to where they're sparse, is called diffusion. It's a zigzag commute, not a sprint.

title: Recycling Plastic
objective: After this level you can explain what happens to plastic when it is recycled.
summary: Thermoplastics remelt; thermosets don't. Recycling sorts, grinds, washes and melts plastic into pellets, sorting flakes by density. Broken polymer chains lower the quality.

cards.headline: Heat one plastic and it melts. Heat another and it never will.
cards.body: Thermoplastics soften and can be remelted. Thermosets can't. That single difference decides whether a plastic can be melted down and made into something new.

cards.headline: Melters and non-melters
cards.body: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, which makes them readily recyclable. Thermosets, such as epoxy and polyurethane, cross-link as they harden. Once set, they can't be remelted; old thermosets are usually ground up and used as filler. As an analogy: one is chocolate, the other is a baked cake.

cards.headline: From bottle to pellet
cards.body: Mechanical recycling runs like a production line. Plastic is sorted by type, ground into small flakes and washed with hot water and detergent. Then the flakes are melted and formed into pellets, the raw material for new products.

cards.headline: Sorted by floating
cards.body: One step is pure Level 8. Flakes go into a water tank and separate by density. PET flakes from bottles sink, while flakes from caps, made of polypropylene or HDPE, float. Denser than water sinks; less dense floats. Density does the sorting, no robot needed.

cards.headline: Why recycled isn't quite new
cards.body: The heat and grinding of recycling break some of plastic's long polymer chains. So recycled plastic usually doesn't match new plastic, and it often goes into less-demanding products. Every trip through the melter costs it a little.

title: Glass From Sand
objective: After this level you can explain how glass is made from sand.
summary: Glass is sand (silica) melted with soda, which lowers the melting temperature, and lime, which stops it dissolving in water. Cooled fast, it becomes an amorphous solid; it doesn't slowly flow.

cards.headline: Your window started out as sand.
cards.body: Everyday glass is made from sand plus two helpers, limestone and soda. Turning a gritty beach into something you can see through takes serious heat and a little clever chemistry.

cards.headline: Sand is hard to melt
cards.body: Sand is silicon dioxide, also called silica, and it melts only above 1,700 °C. So glassmakers add soda (sodium carbonate), which works as a flux: it lowers the melting temperature dramatically. Soda is the shortcut.

cards.headline: The catch: glass that dissolves
cards.body: Silica and soda alone make a glass that dissolves in water. Not ideal for a window in the rain. So glassmakers add a third ingredient, lime (calcium oxide, from limestone), which makes the glass insoluble again. Sand, soda and lime: soda-lime glass.

cards.headline: A solid with no pattern
cards.body: Molten glass is cooled quickly enough that crystals never form. Remember Level 3: in a solid, particles are tightly packed, often in a regular pattern. Glass skips the pattern. Its particles freeze in a jumble, making it an amorphous solid: rigid, but without a crystal's long-range order.

mascot.line: Checked the windows. Still solid. Still not dripping.

cards.headline: The flowing-window myth
cards.body: You may have heard that glass is a very slow liquid, because some old windows are thicker at the bottom. It isn't. Those panes were made uneven to begin with. Room-temperature glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably. Your windows aren't dripping; they're just old.
