title: Fuels
objective: After this level you can explain how gasoline and natural gas store energy.
summary: Fuels store chemical energy in their bonds and release it as heat. Gasoline and natural gas are hydrocarbons; natural gas is mostly methane, and gasoline is distilled from crude oil.

cards.headline: Natural gas has no smell. The smell is added on purpose.
cards.body: Natural gas is colorless and odorless, so gas companies add mercaptan, a chemical with a strong, unpleasant smell. That way a leak announces itself: Level 86's airborne chemicals, drafted as an alarm. And that gas is a remarkable way to store energy.

cards.headline: Energy stored in bonds
cards.body: Fuels hold chemical energy: energy stored in the bonds of atoms and molecules. Petroleum and natural gas are packed with it. Burning converts it to heat, whether it's a gas flame under a pot or gasoline in a car engine. A full tank is really a tank of stored bonds.

cards.headline: Hydrocarbons: carbon and hydrogen
cards.body: Petroleum and natural gas are made mainly of hydrocarbons, compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4), the simplest one: one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. When hydrocarbons burn, they form carbon dioxide and water, the same products as Level 9's burning candle.

cards.headline: Made from ancient life
cards.body: Where did all that stored energy come from? Oil and natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, buried and changed by heat and pressure. Filling a tank means burning very old leftovers.

cards.headline: Gasoline: distilled from crude oil
cards.body: Gasoline is made from crude oil at refineries, and the first step is Level 7's trick on a giant scale: distillation. Heated crude oil separates into fractions by boiling point inside a tall tower. The lightest fractions, gasoline among them, rise to the top.

cards.body: In some homes, soap leaves a gray scum on the tub and seems to clean less well. The water is to blame. Then step into one kitchen and find the whole chapter at once.

mascot.line: Same two-ended trick, better manners around calcium.

cards.headline: Detergents: soap's synthetic cousins
cards.body: Detergents work like soap, with a charged head and a long oil-attracting tail. But they're made from petroleum products instead of natural fats, and they don't form scum with calcium and magnesium. So they keep cleaning in hard water.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one kitchen

title: Alchemy
objective: After this level you can explain what alchemists tried to do and what they got right.
summary: Alchemists chased gold and long life and never caught either. Along the way they built the tools of the lab, like the alembic still, and gave chemistry its very name.

cards.headline: Isaac Newton wrote about a million words on alchemy.
cards.body: The man who explained gravity spent some thirty years on it, mostly in secret. So what were alchemists chasing, and was any of it worth the effort?

cards.headline: The dream: gold, and a longer life
cards.body: Alchemists tried to turn base metals, such as lead or copper, into silver or gold. Many hoped to make the philosophers' stone, a material that was supposed to do the transforming for them. A second dream ran alongside: a cure for disease and a way to extend life. Big goals. As it turned out, what they built while chasing them mattered far more.

mascot.line: Filtering, subliming, distilling. The alchemists had the moves; they just wanted the wrong prize.

cards.headline: The toolkit they left behind
cards.body: Alchemists described apparatus for distillation, sublimation and filtration in careful detail. Their alembic was a still in three parts: a vessel to heat the mixture, a head to catch and cool the vapor, and a receiver for the liquid that dripped out. Remember Level 7? Distilling works because the parts of a mixture boil at different temperatures. Three Chapter 1 moves were already on the alchemist's bench.

cards.headline: Words that stuck around
cards.body: The word alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kimiya, and the word chemistry grew out of alchemy. Arabic alchemy handed down alcohol, elixir and alembic too. And an ancient alchemist named Maria is credited with gentle heating in a bath of hot water instead of an open flame. Her name survives in the cook's bain-marie. The gold never came. The lab did.
cards.callout: Chemistry's name, tools and techniques all passed through the alchemist's workshop.

title: Robert Boyle
objective: After this level you can explain Boyle's work on gases.
summary: Boyle found a trapped gas's volume is inversely proportional to its pressure: half the space, twice the push. He championed experiment, and was still an alchemist.

cards.headline: Block the end of a syringe and push. The air pushes back.
cards.body: Press the plunger in and the trapped air resists harder the further you go. Squeeze it into half the space and it pushes back twice as hard. In 1662 Robert Boyle published the rule behind that push.

cards.headline: A pump, a partner and a rule
cards.body: In 1659 Boyle and Robert Hooke finished building an air pump and used it to study air. From those experiments came the rule Boyle published in 1662, now called Boyle's law: at a constant temperature, a gas's volume is inversely proportional to its pressure. Double the pressure and the volume halves. Halve the pressure and the gas swells to twice its volume.
cards.callout: Boyle's law: more pressure, less volume, at the same temperature.

mascot.line: Breathe in. Congratulations, you just ran Boyle's experiment.

cards.headline: Why gases give way
cards.body: Level 3 explains why this works for gases. Their particles are far apart and move freely, so there is room to crowd them closer. Liquids and solids have almost no room to spare: their volume barely changes under pressure. You use Boyle's law with every breath. Your chest expands, the volume in your lungs grows, the pressure inside drops, and air flows in.

cards.headline: The skeptical chemist
cards.body: Boyle's 1661 book The Sceptical Chymist attacked the old Aristotelian ideas about what matter is made of. His work leaned on experiment and observation, and he argued so hard for chemistry that he was later called the father of chemistry.

cards.headline: A founder with a secret hobby
cards.body: Yet Boyle, like Newton in Level 91, pursued alchemy all his life, still hoping to turn base metals into gold. Science didn't switch on overnight. Its founders carried one foot in the old workshop and one in the new lab.

title: Lavoisier
objective: After this level you can explain how Lavoisier founded modern chemistry.
summary: Lavoisier showed burned metals gain oxygen, ending phlogiston, named oxygen and hydrogen, helped create chemistry's naming system and listed 33 elements, light and heat among them.

cards.headline: In 1789, Lavoisier listed 33 elements. Light and heat made the list.
cards.body: It was the best list anyone had, and it still had two entries that aren't substances at all. How did Antoine Lavoisier earn the title father of modern chemistry, and what did he get wrong?

cards.headline: Goodbye, phlogiston
cards.body: Before Lavoisier, many chemists believed that burnable things, like charcoal and metals, contained phlogiston, which they released into the air as they burned. But metals such as lead and tin weigh more after burning, not less. Lavoisier showed why: oxygen from the air combines with the metal. Level 2 told you air has mass. Take some in, and you get heavier.

mascot.line: "Dephlogisticated air" versus "oxygen". I know which one I'd rather spell.

cards.headline: Names that say what's inside
cards.body: In 1787 Lavoisier and three colleagues published a new method for naming chemical substances. Out went old names like dephlogisticated air and inflammable air. In came oxygen, meaning acid former, and hydrogen, meaning water former, because Lavoisier had shown that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. With small changes, that system is still the basis of chemical names today.

cards.headline: The list, the partner, the guillotine
cards.body: His 1789 textbook listed 33 substances he considered elements, starting with light and caloric (heat), which aren't elements at all. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked beside him, drawing his laboratory for the book and translating English research. His day job undid him. He held a share in a tax-collecting company, and during the Reign of Terror he was guillotined, on May 8, 1794.

title: Dalton's Atoms
objective: After this level you can explain Dalton's atomic theory.
summary: Watching the weather led John Dalton to atoms: every element has its own atom with its own mass, compounds join atoms in whole-number ratios, and reactions only rearrange atoms.

cards.headline: For 57 years, John Dalton wrote down the weather every day.
cards.body: He started in 1787 and kept going until his death in 1844. That habit, of all things, led him to the atom.

mascot.line: 57 years of weather notes. And you thought your diary habit was impressive.

cards.headline: From weather to atoms
cards.body: Weather happens in the air, and Level 6 told you air is a solution of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Dalton studied how those gases share the sky. He concluded that each gas in a mixture pushes independently, exerting its own pressure as if the others weren't there. Thinking about gases that way led him, by way of meteorology, to atoms.

cards.headline: The theory in four lines
cards.body: Starting in 1808, Dalton set out his theory in A New System of Chemical Philosophy. All matter is made of tiny atoms. Each element has its own kind of atom, with its own characteristic mass. Compounds are atoms of different elements joined in small whole-number ratios. And in a chemical change, atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged. Level 9's new substances? Same atoms, new partners.
cards.callout: Level 3 said matter is made of particles. Dalton is a big reason we say so.

cards.headline: Wrong formula, right idea
cards.body: Dalton wasn't right about everything. He wrote water as HO, one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom. In fact water has hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 to 1 ratio: H2O. Notice what the fix kept, though. It's still atoms of two elements in a small whole-number ratio, just as his theory said.

title: Marie Curie
objective: After this level you can explain Curie's discovery of radium and polonium.
summary: Marie Curie named radioactivity, found polonium and radium hiding in pitchblende, purified a tenth of a gram of radium from tons of ore, and won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

cards.headline: Several tons of ore. One tenth of a gram of prize.
cards.body: That was Marie Curie's haul after thousands of rounds of purifying radium. Why would anyone go to such lengths for so little?

cards.headline: A rock that was too active
cards.body: Henri Becquerel had found that uranium gives off rays; Curie gave the effect its name, radioactivity. She found that pitchblende, a uranium ore, was much more radioactive than pure uranium itself. Something else in the rock had to be responsible. In 1898 she and Pierre Curie announced two new elements: polonium, named after her native Poland, and radium.

cards.headline: The hardest separation
cards.body: Level 7 separated mixtures by using differences between their parts. Curie's guide was radioactivity itself: each time she removed some of a known element, such as bismuth, what was left was more active. But to prove radium was a real element, she needed enough to show. After thousands of crystallizations from several tons of starting material, she had one decigram, a tenth of a gram, of almost pure radium chloride.
cards.callout: Her detector for the hidden element was the radiation it gave off.

cards.headline: Two prizes, two sciences
cards.body: In 1903 Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone, for discovering radium and polonium. She remains the only woman to win in two different fields. The radiation she studied also harmed her: she died in 1934 of aplastic anemia caused by radiation exposure.

title: Rosalind Franklin
objective: After this level you can explain Franklin's X-ray picture of DNA.
summary: Rosalind Franklin used X-ray diffraction to photograph DNA. Her Photo 51 showed an X that meant a helix. It was shown to Watson without her knowledge, and she died before the 1962 Nobel.

cards.headline: One photograph took 62 hours to expose.
cards.body: In May 1952, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling aimed X-rays at a thin fiber of DNA and waited. The picture they got, Photo 51, helped reveal the shape of DNA.

mascot.line: You can't see an atom. You can see the shadow of a whole army of them marching in step.

cards.headline: Seeing with X-rays
cards.body: Franklin was a chemist who, from 1951 at King's College London, studied DNA with X-ray diffraction. X-rays scatter off a crystal at angles that reveal how its atoms are arranged. Level 3 said the particles in a solid are often packed in a neat, repeating pattern. Order in, pattern out: the scattered X-rays leave a pattern on film that encodes the structure.

cards.headline: X marks the shape
cards.body: Photo 51 showed a bold X-shaped pattern. To Franklin, that X meant DNA's strands are helical, twisted like a spiral staircase (an analogy). The photo became some of the clearest evidence that DNA is a double helix.
cards.callout: The X in Photo 51 is the signature of a helix.

cards.headline: Who got the credit
cards.body: In early 1953, her colleague Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to James Watson, without her knowledge or agreement. That April, Watson and Crick published their DNA model in Nature, and Franklin and Gosling's own paper appeared in the same issue. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared a Nobel Prize, which is never awarded after death.

title: New Materials
objective: After this level you can describe inventions like nylon and nonstick coatings.
summary: Nylon was invented on purpose, in 1935, as a synthetic silk. Teflon was found by accident in 1938, when a cylinder of gas turned into a slippery white solid that nothing sticks to.

cards.headline: Two everyday materials, one company: one found on purpose, one by accident.
cards.body: In 1935 a team at DuPont invented nylon. In 1938 a DuPont chemist opened a gas cylinder, and nothing came out. That was how Teflon began.

cards.headline: Silk you can make in a lab
cards.body: Wallace Carothers's team at DuPont invented nylon in 1935 as a synthetic silk. It was a useful fiber built by chemistry from compounds available from air, water, and coal or petroleum: no silkworms required. Nylon went into production in 1939, and nylon stockings were a sensation at that year's New York World's Fair. In World War II, nylon went into parachutes instead.

mascot.line: When the scale disagrees with your eyes, trust the scale.

cards.headline: The cylinder that wasn't empty
cards.body: In 1938 Roy Plunkett had stored tetrafluoroethylene gas in small cylinders. When he opened one, no gas came out, yet it weighed the same as before. Level 2 explains why that was a clue: the matter was still in there, mass and all. Inside he found a white powder. The gas had turned into a new solid substance, a chemical change straight out of Level 9.

cards.headline: Why nothing sticks
cards.body: Plunkett tested the powder. It resisted heat, reacted with almost nothing, and was so slippery that most substances wouldn't stick to it. We know it as Teflon. Its first uses were industrial; nonstick pans came years later. One discovery was planned, the other was noticed, and both started with a chemist paying attention.

title: Green Chemistry
objective: After this level you can explain how chemists make processes safer and cleaner.
summary: Green chemistry designs out hazardous substances instead of cleaning them up later. Atom economy keeps starting materials in the product, as in a three-step ibuprofen route.

cards.headline: The cleanest way to handle hazardous waste? Never make it.
cards.body: That's the idea behind green chemistry. It changes the question from "How do we clean this up?" to "Why are we making it at all?"

cards.headline: Prevent, don't mop up
cards.body: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances. That's different from cleanup, which treats waste after it's made, often by separating hazardous chemicals from everything else: a Level 7 job, on an industrial scale. Green chemistry works upstream, so there's less to separate in the first place.
cards.callout: Cleanup treats waste after it's made. Green chemistry avoids making it.

mascot.line: Waste few or no atoms. My new motto, and also my approach to cookies.

cards.headline: Twelve principles, starting with waste
cards.body: In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner set out the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry. The first: it's better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up afterward. The second is atom economy: design reactions so the final product contains as much of the starting materials as possible. Picture a recipe where most of the ingredients go in the bin instead of the cake (an analogy). Atom economy keeps them in the cake.

cards.headline: The ibuprofen fix
cards.body: An older way of making ibuprofen, the everyday painkiller, took six steps, and under 40 percent of the atoms used ended up in the product. BHC Company found a route with three steps and about 80 percent. It also recovers and reuses its main byproduct. In 1997 the route won a US Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award.

title: Chemistry Myths
objective: After this level you can debunk myths, like "chemical-free" products.
summary: Everything is made of chemicals, so nothing is chemical-free: a 2008 million-pound offer and a blank 2014 'overview' made the point. And a molecule is the same from fruit or factory.

cards.headline: In 2008, chemists offered a million pounds for anything 100% chemical-free.
cards.body: The Royal Society of Chemistry promised the money to the first member of the public who could hand over such a material. Why were they so relaxed about it?

cards.headline: Everything is chemicals
cards.body: Everything you eat, drink and live in is made of chemicals, natural and synthetic alike. Level 2 said matter is anything with mass that takes up space, and Level 1 said chemistry studies what matter is made of. A truly chemical-free product would have to be made of nothing at all. The Royal Society of Chemistry was reclaiming the word from advertising, where chemical had come to mean poison.

mascot.line: Fastest peer review of my life. I read the whole results section in zero seconds.

cards.headline: A paper with nothing in it
cards.body: In 2014 two chemists sent the journal Nature Chemistry "A comprehensive overview of chemical-free consumer products". They examined lotions, supplements, household cleaners, foods and drinks, then listed every product that truly deserved the label. The list was empty. The journal shared the paper on its blog.

cards.headline: Natural isn't a different molecule
cards.body: A related myth says synthetic versions are chemically different from natural ones. Vitamin C says otherwise: natural and synthetic vitamin C are chemically identical, with no known difference in how they act in your body. A molecule doesn't remember whether it came from fruit or a factory. What matters is which substance it is, not where it was made.
